I really do appreciate the backstory. It makes the question more interesting. Anyways…

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>There is this geometric property (I don't know what its called) that if you have a rectangle, and a point inside the rectangle, and you draw lines from the corners to this point (let's say the distances are a,b,c, and d, clockwise), then a^2+c^2=b^2+d^2. If you plug in a combination of the numbers 9, 15, and 16, you will see that the equation 15^2+16^2=9^2+d^2 will give you the integer value of d. Solving, we get d=20.</details>

Also if you didn't know British Flag Theorem, you could always set up a system of equations and just do elimination to find one of the lengths.

stem_md:
Of the thirteen members of the volunteer group, Hannah selects herself, Tom Morris, Jerry Hsu, Thelma Paterson, and Louise Bueller to teach the September classes.  When she is done, she decides that it's not necessary to balance the number of female and male teachers with the proportions of girls and boys at the hospital  $\textit{every}$  month, and having half the women work while only  $2$  of the  $7$  men work on some months means that some of the women risk getting burned out.  After all, nearly all the members of the volunteer group have other jobs.

Hannah comes up with a plan that the committee likes.  Beginning in October, the comittee of five volunteer teachers will consist of any five members of the volunteer group, so long as there is at least one woman and at least one man teaching each month.  Under this new plan, what is the least number of months that  $\textit{must}$  go by (including October when the first set of five teachers is selected, but not September) such that some five-member comittee  $\textit{must have}$  taught together twice (all five members are the same during two different months)?
solution_md: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We count how many possible different committees there are. There are 6 women and 7 men, and the number of committees without restrictions is  $\dbinom{13}{5} = 1287$ . The number of committees with only women is  $\dbinom{6}{5} = 6$  and the number of committees with only men is  $\dbinom{7}{5} = 21$  (this is the complement). So, the total number of committees is  $1287-6-21=1260$ . To guarantee that one group will have taught twice, by the Pigeonhole Principle,  $\boxed{1261}$  months must have gone by.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/ITest/2008 ITest/535972.json

solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>subtracting the first eqiation form the last, we get  $x_2+x_3+\cdots+x_{2008}=-2008$ Similarly,  $x_1+x_3+\cdots+x_{2008}=-2007$ and so on until  $x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_{2007}=-1$ We add all these equations to get  $2007x_1+2007x_2+\cdots+2007x_{2008}=-\frac{2008\times2009}{2}$ And so the sum of all the terms equals  $-\frac{2008\times2009}{2\times2007}$ .

Michael notices that the first four digits of  $987-1234$  descend  $(9-8-7-1)$  and that the last four ascend in order  $(1-2-3-4)$ . Michael then wonders to himself how many businesses in a single area code could have such phone numbers.  How many  $7$ -digit telephone numbers are there such that all seven digits are distinct, the first four digits are in descending order, and the last four digits are in ascending order?

"Ew, landfill gas!" Alexis complains mockingly.

Wanting to save her own energy, Alexis decides to take a nap.  She falls asleep and dreams of walking around a  $2-\text{D}$  coordinate grid, looking for a wormhole that she believes will transport her to the beach (bypassing the time spent in the family van).  In her dream, Alexis finds herself holding a device that she recognizes as a  $\textit{tricorder}$  from one of the old  $\textit{Star Trek}$  t.v. series.  The tricorder has a button labeled "wormhole" and when Alexis presses the button, a computerized voice from the tricorder announces, "You are at the origin.  Distance to the wormhole is  $2400$  units.  Your wormhole distance allotment is  $\textit{two}$ ."'

Unsure as to how to reach, Alexis begins walking forward.  As she walks, the tricorder displays at all times her distance from her starting point at the origin.  When Alexis is  $2400$  units from the origin, she again presses the "wormhole" buttom.  The same computerized voice as before begins, "Distance to the origin is  $2400$  units.  Distance to the wormhole is  $3840$  units.  Your wormhole distance allotment is  $\textit{two}$ ."

Alexis begins to feel disoriented.  She wonders what is means that her  $\textit{wormhole distance allotment is two}$ , and why that number didn't change as she pushed the button.  She puts her hat down to mark her position, then wanders aroud a bit.  The tricorder shows her two readings as she walks.  The first she recognizes as her distance to the origin.  The second reading clearly indicates her distance from the point where her hat lies - where she last pressed the button that gave her distance to the wormhole.

Alexis picks up her hat and begins walking around.  Eventually Alexis finds herself at a spot  $2400$  units from the origin and  $3840$  units from where she last pressed the button.  Feeling hopeful, Alexis presses the tricorder's wormhole button again.  Nothing happens.  She presses it again, and again nothing happens.  "Oh," she thinks, "my wormhole allotment was  $\textit{two}$ , and I used it up already!"

Despair fills poor Alexis who isn't sure what a wormhole looks like or how she's supposed to find it.  Then she takes matters into her own hands.  Alexis sits down and scribbles some notes and realizes where the wormhole must be.  Alexis gets up and runs straight from her "third position" to the wormhole.  As she gets closer, she sees the wormhole, which looks oddly like a huge scoop of icecream.  Alexis runs into the wormhole, then wakes up.

How many units did Alexis run from her third position to the wormhole?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>As jellymoop suggests, let the origin, second location, third location, and wormhole be  $I$ ,  $P_1$ ,  $P_2$ , and  $W$  respectively.  We can construct the following diagram:

[asy]
size(200);
defaultpen(linewidth(0.8));
path circ1=circle(origin,2400),circ2=circle((2400,0),3840);
pair x[]=intersectionpoints(circ1,circ2);
draw(origin--(2400,0)--x[0]--origin--x[1]--(2400,0));
draw(x[0]--x[1],linetype("4 4"));
label(" $2400$ ",(1200,0),N);
label(" $2400$ ",x[0]/2,dir(15));
label(" $2400$ ",x[1]/2,dir(-15));
label(" $3800$ ",(x[0]+(2400,0))/2,dir(45));
label(" $3800$ ",(x[1]+(2400,0))/2,dir(-45));
label(" $I$ ",origin,W);
label(" $P_1$ ",(2400,0),E);
label(" $P_2$ ",x[1],S);
label(" $W$ ",x[0],N);
[/asy]

(Convince yourself that this diagram accurately represents the story told.)

Let  $H$  be the foot of the altitude from  $I$  to  $WP_1$ .  By the Pythagorean Theorem, we have \[IH=\sqrt{IP_1^2-P_1H^2}=\sqrt{2400^2-1920^2}=1440.\]  Next, let  $P$  be the intersection of line segments  $IP_1$  and  $WP_2$ .  Note that by comparing areas, we have that \[IH\cdot WP_1=IP_1\cdot WP\implies WP=\dfrac{IH\cdot WP_1}{IP_1}=\dfrac{1440\cdot3800}{2400}=2304.\]  This implies that  $WP_2=2(WP)=\boxed{4608}$  units.</details>

Finished with rereading Isaac Asimov's  $\textit{Foundation}$  series, Joshua asks his father, "Do you think somebody will build small devices that run on nuclear energy while I'm alive?"

"Honestly, Josh, I don't know.  There are a lot of very different engineering problems involved in designing such devices.  But technology moves forward at an amazing pace, so I won't tell you we can't get there in time for you to see it.  I  $\textit{did}$  go to a graduate school with a lady who now works on  $\textit{portable}$  nuclear reactors.  They're not small exactly, but they aren't nearly as large as most reactors.  That might be the first step toward a nuclear-powered pocket-sized video game.

Hannah adds, "There are already companies designing batteries that are nuclear in the sense that they release energy from uranium hydride through controlled exoenergetic processes.  This process is not the same as the nuclear fission going on in today's reactors, but we can certainly call it  $\textit{nuclear energy}$ ."

"Cool!" Joshua's interest is piqued.

Hannah continues, "Suppose that right now in the year  $2008$  we can make one of these nuclear batteries in a battery shape that is  $2$  meters  $\textit{across}$ .  Let's say you need that size to be reduced to  $2$  centimeters  $\textit{across}$ , in the same proportions, in order to use it to run your little video game machine.  If every year we reduce the necessary volume of such a battery by  $1/3$ , in what year will the batteries first get small enough?"

Joshua asks, "The battery shapes never change?  Each year the new batteries are similar in shape - in all dimensions - to the bateries from previous years?"

"That's correct," confirms Joshua's mother.  "Also, the base  $10$  logarithm of  $5$  is about  $0.69897$  and the base  $10$  logarithm of  $3$  is around  $0.47712$ ."  This makes Joshua blink.  He's not sure he knows how to use logarithms, but he does think he can compute the answer.  He correctly notes that after  $13$  years, the batteries will already be barely more than a sixth of their original width.

Assuming Hannah's prediction of volume reduction is correct and effects are compounded continuously, compute the first year that the nuclear batteries get small enough for pocket video game machines.  Assume also that the year  $2008$  is  $7/10$  complete.

My SolutionDrop the altitude from the vertex opposite $x$ to the side whose length is $x$ . Call this height $h$ . Then, from the Pythagorean Theorem, $h=\sqrt{65^2-\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2}$ . Then, the area of the triangle is \[ A = \dfrac {xh}{2} = \dfrac {x \cdot \sqrt{65^2-\dfrac{x^2}{4}}}{2}. \]We want this to be a positive integer, so we want $ x \cdot \sqrt {65^2 - \dfrac{x^2}{4}} $ to be a positive even integer. Simplify this: \[ \begin {align*} x \cdot \sqrt {65^2 - \dfrac{x^2}{4}} &= x \cdot \sqrt {\dfrac {4 \cdot 65^2 - x^2}{4}} &= \dfrac {x \cdot \sqrt {4 \cdot 65^2 - x^2}}{2}. \]Remember, we want this to be even, so we want $ x \cdot \sqrt {4 \cdot 65^2 - x^2} $ to be a multiple of $4$ . Since I hate typing $ 4 \cdot 65^2 $ every time, note that \[ 4 \cdot 65^2 = 2^2 \cdot 65^2 = (2 \cdot 65)^2 = 130^2. \]Nice! This means $x$ could be at most $130$ . But this gives $0$ area, because that's a degenerate triangle. So we omit that solution. Note, from the Intermediate Values Theorem (thanks to **[bdejean](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/memberlist.php?mode=viewprofile&u=52577)**) for helping me clear this confusion up, that each perfect square between the minimum and maximum is achieved, because our function is monotonously continuously increasing/decreasing. The minimum value for $x$ is $x=0$ , but this is meaningless. The maximum value of $x$ is $x=130$ , but this is meaningless. We use Calculus. Let $ A(x) = x \cdot \sqrt {130^2 - x^2} $ . Then: $ A'(x) = -\dfrac{2\left(x^2-\dfrac{130^2}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{130^2-x^2}} $ One can easily check the above using the Chain and Product Rules for Derivatives. We see that $A'(x)=0$ wwhen $x=\dfrac{130^2}{2}$ . From here, we backtrack and find $A(x)$ at this point. We obtain: \[ \begin {align*} A \left( \dfrac {130^2}{2} \right) &= \dfrac {130^2}{2} \cdot \sqrt {130^2}{2} &= \dfrac {130^3}{2\sqrt{2}}. \]Using a Calculator, we see that this is approximately $776756.8$ . Therefore, since this is the maximum, all integer areas from $1$ to $776756$ are possible. One can easily see a one-to-one bijection by graphing. Therefore, there are $\fbox{776756}$ possible values of $x$ . **Remark**: We are given that the triangle is isosceles, which, unless under very unusual and extraordinary circumstances, excludes equilaterality (if that's a word). We did not count this bogus solution because the area would be non-integral.

Alexis and Joshua are walking along the beach when they decide to draw symbols in the sand.  Alex draws only stars and only draws them in pairs while Joshua draws only squares in trios.  "Let's see how many rows of  $15$  adjacent symbols we can make this way," suggests Josh.  Alexis is game for the task and the two get busy drawing.  Some of their rows look like 

\[\begin{array}{ccccccccccccccc} \vspace{10pt}*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare\vspace{10pt}\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*&*\vspace{10pt}\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&*&*&*&*&*&*&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare \vspace{10pt}\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare\vspace{10pt} *&*&*&*&*&*&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&\blacksquare&*&*&*&*&*&*\end{array}\] 
The twins decide to count each of the first two rows above as distinct rows, even though one is the mirror image of the other.  But the last of the rows above is its own mirror image, so they count it only once.  Around an hour later, the twins realized that they had drawn every possible row exactly once using their rules of stars in pairs and squares in trips.  How many rows did they draw in the sand?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Since there are an odd number of adjacent symbols, there can only be an odd number of the square triplets. 
If there is an even number of triplets, say 2, then there will be an odd number of symbol 'spots' left, which can't be covered with pairs of stars. 
So, the only possible number of triplets are 1, 3 and 5 and the corresponding number of star triplets will be 6, 3 and 0.
counting the cases separately,
<details><summary>Case 1: Square Triplets:1, Star Pairs:6</summary>We have  $\dbinom{7}{6}=7$  ways to arrange them(7 ways to place the Square triplet and the others go to the remaining spots)</details>
<details><summary>Case 2: Square Triplets:3, Star Pairs:3</summary>We have  $\dbinom{6}{3}=20$  ways of arranging (20 ways to choose where to put the square triplets and he rest go in the other spots)</details>
<details><summary>Case 3: Square Triplets:5, Star Pairs:0</summary>We have  $\dbinom{5}{5}=1$  ways of arranging</details>
and so we have a total of  $20+7+1=\boxed{28}$</details>

solution_md: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Grouping alike terms, the  $n$ -th group has  $n$  terms, the last term has value  $n(3n-1)/2$  and is the global term  $n(n+1)/2.$ Let  $n(n+1)/2=2008, n=62.8, u_{2008}$  locates in the  $63$ -th group, the last term is  $u_{2016}.$  $u_{2008}$  is  $8$  terms before it, so  $u_{2008}=63(3*63-1)/2-3*8=\boxed{5898.}$</details>

After swimming around the ocean with some snorkling gear, Joshua walks back to the beach where Alexis works on a mural in the sand beside where they drew out symbol lists.  Joshua walks directly over the mural without paying any attention.

"You're a square, Josh."

"No,  $\textit{you're}$  a square," retorts Joshua.  "In fact, you're a  $\textit{cube}$ , which is  $50\%$  freakier than a square by dimension.  And before you tell me I'm a hypercube, I'll remind you that mom and dad confirmed that they could not have given birth to a four dimension being."

"Okay, you're a cubist caricature of male immaturity," asserts Alexis.

Knowing nothing about cubism, Joshua decides to ignore Alexis and walk to where he stashed his belongings by a beach umbrella.  He starts thinking about cubes and computes some sums of cubes, and some cubes of sums: \begin{align*}1^3+1^3+1^3&=3,1^3+1^3+2^3&=10,1^3+2^3+2^3&=17,2^3+2^3+2^3&=24,1^3+1^3+3^3&=29,1^3+2^3+3^3&=36,(1+1+1)^3&=27,(1+1+2)^3&=64,(1+2+2)^3&=125,(2+2+2)^3&=216,(1+1+3)^3&=125,(1+2+3)^3&=216.\end{align*}  Josh recognizes that the cubes of the sums are always larger than the sum of cubes of positive integers.  For instance, 

\begin{align*}(1+2+4)^3&=1^3+2^3+4^3+3(1^2\cdot 2+1^2\cdot 4+2^2\cdot 1+2^2\cdot 4+4^2\cdot 1+4^2\cdot 2)+6(1\cdot 2\cdot 4)&>1^3+2^3+4^3.\end{align*}

Josh begins to wonder if there is a smallest value of  $n$  such that \[(a+b+c)^3\leq n(a^3+b^3+c^3)\] for all natural numbers  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$ .  Joshua thinks he has an answer, but doesn't know how to prove it, so he takes it to Michael who confirms Joshua's answer with a proof.  What is the correct value of  $n$  that Joshua found?

So  $n = \boxed{9}$  should work (checking endpoints is important).</details>

As the Kubiks head homeward, away from the beach in the family van, Jerry decides to take a different route away from the beach than the one they took to get there.  The route involves lots of twists and turns, prompting Hannah to wonder aloud if Jerry's "shortcut" will save any time at all.

Michael offers up a problem as an analogy to his father's meandering: "Suppose dad drives around, making right-angled turns after  $\textit{every}$  mile.  What is the farthest he could get us from our starting point after driving us  $500$  miles assuming that he makes exactly  $300$  right turns?"

"Sounds almost like an energy efficiency problem," notes Hannah only half jokingly.  Hannah is always encouraging her children to think along these lines.

Let  $d$  be the answer to Michael's problem.  Compute  $\lfloor d\rfloor$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>The Doctor's Solution</summary>Let the number of units north be  $a$  and the number of units west be  $b$ . Clearly,  $a+b\le500$  and  $a,b\ge150$ .  $d$  should be the maximum value of  $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ .

For simplicity, let's instead maximize  $a^2+b^2=\left(a+b\right)^2-2\cdot a\cdot b\le250000-2\cdot a\cdot b$ . Now we're minimizing  $a\cdot b$ .

We can assume  $a+b=500$ ; otherwise either  $a$  or  $b$  is smaller than it needs to be and so  $a^2+b^2$  is smaller than it needs to be. Then we're minimizing  $a\cdot\left(500-a\right)$ . The First Derivative Test gives us local extrema of  $\pm250$ , and  $250$  is a local maximum, by the Second Derivative Test. Thus the global extrema occur on the endpoints of our interval, or  $\left(150,350\right)$  and  $\left(350,150\right)$ . Thus our final answer is  $\boxed{\left\lfloor\sqrt{150^2+350^2}\right\rfloor}$ , which ... I have yet to simplify.</details>

stem_md:
With about six hours left on the van ride home from vacation, Wendy looks for something to do.  She starts working on a project for the math team.

There are sixteen students, including Wendy, who are about to be sophomores on the math team.  Elected as a math team officer, one of Wendy's jobs is to schedule groups of the sophomores to tutor geometry students after school on Tuesdays.  The way things have been done in the past, the same number of sophomores tutor every week, but the same group of students never works together.  Wendy notices that there are even numbers of groups she could select whether she chooses  $4$  or  $5$  students at a time to tutor geometry each week:
\begin{align*}\dbinom{16}4&=1820,\dbinom{16}5&=4368.\end{align*} 
Playing around a bit more, Wendy realizes that unless she chooses all or none of the students on the math team to tutor each week that the number of possible combinations of the sophomore math teamers is always even.  This gives her an idea for a problem for the  $2008$  Jupiter Falls High School Math Meet team test:

\[\text{How many of the 2009 numbers on Row 2008 of Pascal's Triangle are even?}\]

Wendy works the solution out correctly.  What is her answer?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>This, besides all the nonsense..., is a specific case for Lucas's Theorem. $2009 = 11111011000_2$ Now it is easily proven by induction that  $(x+1)^{2N} \equiv x^{2N}+1 \pmod {2}$ Therefore,

\[(x+1)^{2009} = (x+1)^{2^{10}}(x+1)^{2^9}(x+1)^{2^8}(x+1)^{2^7}(x+1)^{2^6}(x+1)^{2^4}(x+1)^{2^3} \equiv\]
\[ (x^{1024}+1)(x^{512}+1)(x^{256}+1)(x^{128}+1)(x^{64}+1)(x^{16}+1)(x^8+1) \pmod 2\]

Since there isnt any way to get a coefficient twice, there are  $2^7 = \boxed{128}$  odd numbers.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/ITest/2008 ITest/536355.json

stem_md:
Feeling excited over her successful explorations into Pascal's Triangle, Wendy formulates a second problem to use during a future Jupiter Falls High School Math Meet:

\[\text{How many of the first 2010 rows of Pascal's Triangle (Rows 0 through 2009)} \ \text{have exactly 256 odd entries?}\]
What is the solution to Wendy's second problem?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Say we are looking at row  $n$ . Let  $n = \overline{a_ma_{m-1} \cdots a_0}_2$  Now define a new set of   $b_i$  composed entirely of  $1's$  from  $a_i$ .

 Now combining this with the fact that  $(x+1)^{2a} \equiv x^{2a}+1 \pmod 2$ , we have: $(x+1)^n = \prod (x+1)^{2^ib_i} \equiv \prod(x^{2^ib_i}+1) \pmod 2$ Since there is only one unique way to write a number in base  $2$  (and any for that matter), there is only one way to get a specific power in our expansion.

Therefore, the number of odd entries are simply  $2^t \implies t = 8$  where  $t = |b_i|$ . Therefore,  $n$  must originally have  $8$   $1's$  and the rest  $0's$  when written in base  $2$ .

Now  $2010 = 11111011010_2 $ Thus, our final answer is  $\dbinom{11}{3}-\dbinom{5}{2} = \boxed{155}$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/ITest/2008 ITest/536356.json

solution_md: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>$p(x)=q(x)(x^2+1)(x^2+x+1)+r(x)$  where  $r(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$  $p(i)=r(i);1=d-b+(c-a)i;d-b=1,c-a=0$  $p(\omega)=r(\omega);-\omega^2=a+b\omega^2+c\omega+d$  $p(\omega^2)=r(\omega^2);-\omega=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d$  $a=c=d=0,b=-1,r(x)=-x^2,|r(2008)|=2008^2=64\mod1000.$</details>

stem_md: Find the greatest natural number  $n$  such that  $n\leq 2008$  and \[(1^2+2^2+3^2+\cdots + n^2)\left[(n+1)^2+(n+2)^2+(n+3)^2+\cdots + (2n)^2\right]\] is a perfect square.
solution_md: Sorry for the revive, but here's a solution, now that I *finally* know how to do this with complete rigor after more than five years. As previous posters have stated, the original expression rewrites as \[ \frac{n^2(2n+1)^2(n+1)(7n+1)}{36}. \] This is a perfect square if and only if $(n+1)(7n+1)$ is a perfect square. Let $(n+1)(7n+1) = k^2$ for some positive integer $k$ . Then \[ 7n^2 + 8n + 1 = k^2,\quad\text{or}\quad (7n+4)^2 - 7k^2 = 9. \] Letting $n_0:=7n+4$ , we obtain $n_0^2 - 7k^2 = 9$ , which is a standard generalized Pell equation. Observe that the fundamental solution to $x^2 - 7y^2 = 1$ is $(x,y) = (8,3)$ , corresponding to the unit $u:=8+3\sqrt 7$ in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 7]$ . Then by Theorem 3.3 in [this article]("https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ugradnumthy/pelleqn2.pdf"), all solutions to $x^2 - 7y^2 = 9$ are Pell multiples of some solution $(x,y)$ satisfying \[ |y|\leq \frac{\sqrt{9(8+3\sqrt 7)}}{\sqrt 7}\approx 4.5266. \] The only nonnegative integer solutions to $x^2 - 7y^2 = 9$ when $y\leq 4$ are $(4,1)$ and $(11,4)$ , so all solutions are generated by the elements $4\pm\sqrt 7$ and $11\pm 4\sqrt 7$ . However, \[ \frac{11-4\sqrt 7}{4+\sqrt 7} = u^{-1}\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{11+4\sqrt 7}{4-\sqrt 7} = u, \] so the second set of solutions is actually part of the first set. Therefore, all solutions to this Pell equation are of the form $(4\pm\sqrt 7)(8+3\sqrt 7)^k$ . Finally, remark that \[ \{(4+\sqrt 7)(8+3\sqrt 7)^k:k\geq 0\} = \{4+\sqrt 7,\,\,53+20\sqrt 7,\,\,844+319\sqrt 7,\,\,13451+5084\sqrt 7,\,\,\cdots\} \] and \[ \{(4-\sqrt 7)(8+3\sqrt 7)^k:k\geq 0\} = \{4-\sqrt 7,\,\,11+4\sqrt 7,\,\,172+65\sqrt 7,\,\,2741+1036\sqrt 7,\,\,\cdots\}. \] It is clear that other solutions give values of $n_0$ larger than $7\cdot 2008 + 4 = 14060$ , and so the largest such solution occurs when $7n+4=13451$ , or $n=\boxed{1921}$ .**Remark.** In this case, the two solutions we obtained through our bounding were Pell multiples of each other, so our extra work in determining this second solution was redundant. However, this is not always the case; the article linked above gives the example $x^2 - 7y^2 = 57$ , whose solutions are generated by the two completely different lists \[ \pm(8\pm\sqrt 7)(8+3\sqrt 7)^k\quad\text{and}\quad \pm(13\pm 4\sqrt 7)(8+3\sqrt 7)^k. \] In particular, both expressions above produce different sets of solutions, and so neither one is, by itself, sufficient to enumerate the entire set.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/ITest/2008 ITest/536502.json

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We have:

\[-r-s = b\]
\[rs = 2008b\]
\[\frac{rs}{-r-s} = 2^3 \cdot 251 \implies (r-2008)(s-2008) = 2^6 \cdot 251^2\]

There are  $2 \cdot 7 \cdot 3 = 42$  solutions.

Now suppose that  $r-2008 = k \implies r = 2008+k$  and  $r-2008 = -k \implies r = -k+2008$ . Their sum will be  $4016$ Similarly, this applies to  $s$  as well.

Therefore,  $|S| = 4016 \cdot 42$</details>

stem_md: Let  $(a,b,c,d)$  be a solution to the system  \begin{align*}a+b&=15,ab+c+d&=78,ad+bc&=160,cd&=96.\end{align*}  Find the greatest possible value of  $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ .
solution_md:
Let  $P(x)=(x^2-ax+c)(x^2-bx+d)$ .  Expanding gives $P(x)=x^4-(a+b)x^3+(ab+c+d)x^2-(ad+bc)x+cd=$   $x^4-15x^3+78x^2-160x+96=(x-1)(x-4)^2(x-6)$ .

WLOG  $x-1$  is a factor of  $x^2-ax+c$ .  The other factor is either  $x-4$  or  $x-6$ , so  $(a, b, c, d)=(5, 10, 4, 24)$  with sum of squares 717, or  $(a, b, c, d)=(7, 8, 6, 16)$  with sum of squares 405.  So  $717$  is the greatest.

stem_md: Find the number of  $12$ -digit "words" that can be formed from the alphabet  $\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6\}$  if neighboring digits must differ by exactly  $2$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>If the word starts with an odd digit, all subsequent digits are odd. If it starts with an even digit, all subsequent digits are even.

Now there is one 1-digit word ending in each digit: \[\begin{array}{cccc|ccc}\mathbf{0}&\mathbf{2}&\mathbf{4}&\mathbf{6}&\mathbf{1}&\mathbf{3}&\mathbf{5}\hline 1&1&1&1&1&1&1\end{array}\] The only way that the second digit can be 0 is if the first digit is 2. The only way that the second digit can be 2 is if the first digit is 0 or 4. The only way that the second digit can be 4 is if the first digit is 2 or 6. Continuing, for the second row you get  $1,\ 1+1,\ 1+1,\ 1$  and then  $1,\ 1+1,\ 1$ . \[\begin{array}{cccc|ccc}\mathbf{0}&\mathbf{2}&\mathbf{4}&\mathbf{6}&\mathbf{1}&\mathbf{3}&\mathbf{5}\hline 1&1&1&1&1&1&1\ \ \searrow&\swarrow\searrow&\swarrow\searrow&\swarrow\ \ &\ \ \searrow&\swarrow\searrow&\swarrow\ \ 1&2&2&1&1&2&12&3&3&2&2&2&23&5&5&3&2&4&2\end{array}\] So there are  $3+5+5+3+2+4+2=24$  four-digit words. Continuing to the twelfth row, you get \[\begin{array}{cccc|ccc}\ \ \searrow&\swarrow\searrow&\swarrow\searrow&\swarrow\ \ &\ \ \searrow&\swarrow\searrow&\swarrow\ \ 144&233&233&144&32&64&32\end{array}\] which sums to  $\boxed{882}$ .</details>

stem_md: A six dimensional "cube" (a  $6$ -cube) has  $64$  vertices at the points  $(\pm 3,\pm 3,\pm 3,\pm 3,\pm 3,\pm 3).$   This  $6$ -cube has  $192\text{ 1-D}$  edges and  $240\text{ 2-D}$  edges.  This  $6$ -cube gets cut into  $6^6=46656$  smaller congruent "unit"  $6$ -cubes that are kept together in the tightly packaged form of the original  $6$ -cube so that the  $46656$  smaller  $6$ -cubes share 2-D square faces with neighbors ( $\textit{one}$  2-D square face shared by  $\textit{several}$  unit  $6$ -cube neighbors).  How many 2-D squares are faces of one or more of the unit  $6$ -cubes?
solution_md:
There are a bunch of typos in the question.  Also, is there any particular reason that you're using LaTeX to emphasize text?

Any 2-dimensional face of any of the unit hypercubes lies in one of the 2-dimensional axis-parallel planes that we get by choosing four of the six coordinates and holding them constant.  We have  $\binom{6}{4} = 15$  ways to choose the four coordinates and 7 choices (anything from  $-3$  to  $3$ ) to choose for each, for a total of  $15 \cdot 7^4$  planes.  Once we've fixed this plane we're reduced to the 2-dimensional problem of counting unit squares in a square grid of edge-length 6.  But of course there are exactly  $6^2 = 36$  of these.  So the answer is  $15 \cdot 7^4 \cdot 36$ .

More generally, one can show that the number of  $m$ -dimensional  $1 \times \cdots \times 1$  faces in a division of an  $n$ -dimensional cube of edge-length  $k$  is precisely  $\binom{n}{m} \cdot (k + 1)^{n - m} \cdot k^m$ .

stem_md: For  $a,b,c$  positive reals, let \[N=\dfrac{a^2+b^2}{c^2+ab}+\dfrac{b^2+c^2}{a^2+bc}+\dfrac{c^2+a^2}{b^2+ca}.\]  Find the minimum value of  $\lfloor 2008N\rfloor$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution to this nice problem</summary>We claim that the minimum value of  $N$  is  $3$ . To prove this, note that by AM-GM: $LHS \ge \sum \frac{a^2+b^2}{c^2+\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}}$ Therefore letting  $x=a^2, y=b^2, z=c^2$  and clearing fractions, we must only show that: $\sum \frac{2x+2y}{x+y+2z}\ge 3$ , or $\sum \frac{x+y}{x+y+2z}\ge \frac{3}{2}$ Wlog letting  $x+y+z=1$ , we are left proving: $\sum\frac{1-x}{1+x}\ge \frac{3}{2}$ , which is well-known, and most easily shown with Jensen on  $f(x)=\frac{1-x}{1+x}$ (Edit: Or we can just use Nesbitt  :oops: )

Hence,  $N\ge 3$ , with equality holding iff  $a=b=c$ , so  $\lfloor2008N\rfloor$  (why did they ask for that?) is  $\boxed{6024}$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/ITest/2008 ITest/536509.json

stem_md: For how many positive integers  $n$ ,  $1\leq n\leq 2008$ , can the set \[\{1,2,3,\ldots,4n\}\] be divided into  $n$  disjoint  $4$ -element subsets such that every one of the  $n$  subsets contains the element which is the arithmetic mean of all the elements in that subset?
solution_md:
Here is my solution:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let's set something straight first: if  $a,b,c,d$  are four numbers such that a is the average of them. Then we have  $\frac {a+b+c+d}{4}=a$  which means that the sum is  $a+b+c+d$  is divisible by  $4$ . Since the sum of the all the element in the set is  $\frac {4n(4n+1)}{2}=2n(4n+1)$  and there are  $n$  subsets with the sum of elements that is divisible by  $4$ , we know that  $n$  must be even.
Take  $n=2$ :  $1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8$ . By observation we have two subsets that satisfy:  $(1,3,4,8),(2,5,6,7)$  where  $\frac {1+3+4+8}{4}=4$  and  $ \frac {2+5+6+7}{4}=5$ . Now let's make the numerators  $(9+11+13+16),(10+13+14+15)$ , we do this by adding both sides by  $\frac {4*8}{4} or 8$  and we get  $\frac {9+11+12+16}{4}=4+8=12$  and  $\frac {10+13+14+15}{4}=5+8=13$ , this means that  $(1,3,4,8),(2,5,6,7)(9,11,12,16),(10,13,14,15)$  are the four satisfied subsets in the set  ${1,2,...,16}$ . Thus we can induct that for the set  ${1,2,...,4(2n)}$ , the  $n$  satisfied subsets are  $(1,3,4,8),(2,5,6,7),.....,(1+(n-1)8,3+(n-1)8,4+(n-1)8,8+(n-1)8),  (2+(n-1)8,5+(n-1)8,6+(n-1)8,7+(n-1)8)$ , so there are  $\frac {2008}{2}=1004$  of such n that satisfy the conditions.</details>

During the first week of the 2008-2009 school year at Jupiter Falls High School, the school holds a fire drill.  The  $2008$  students in attendance all leave the school and head for the football field.  Wendy and several of her friends sit down in a circle on the ground and begin to chat.

This leads Lilly's boyfriend Nori to offer up a problem, "Suppose we all stood up and took the space that one of our neighboors had been sitting in.  In how many ways could we do that?"

"I think just four, " offers Wendy, oblivious that Nori is subtly voicing a complaint over Lilly's absence at his side.  "We all either move one spot clockwise, or one spot counterclockwise.  Unless we can sit on each other."

Wendy pulls out a calculator and writes a program that cycles through all the possibilities.  After a couple of minutes she announces, "There are  $31$ .   $\textit{That's}$  a weird number."

"Can you solve it generally?" asks Lilly.

"Honestly, I'm not sure.  I'd need to work on it a bit to know if I could," admits Wendy.

Nori adds more complexity to the problem, "How about this: Let  $k$  be the number of students in a circle.  Then let  $m$  be the number of ways we can rearrange ourselves so that each of us is in the same spot or within one spot of where we started, and no two people are ever in the same spot.  If  $m$  leaves a remainder of  $1$  when divided by  $5$ , how many possible values are there of  $k$ , where  $k$  is at least  $3$  and at most  $2008$ ?"

Find the answer to Nori's problem.

stem_md: Let  $\alpha$  be a root of  $x^6-x-1$ , and call two polynomials  $p$  and  $q$  with integer coefficients  $\textit{equivalent}$  if  $p(\alpha)\equiv q(\alpha)\pmod3$ .  It is known that every such polynomial is equivalent to exactly one of  $0,1,x,x^2,\ldots,x^{727}$ .  Find the largest integer  $n<728$  for which there exists a polynomial  $p$  such that  $p^3-p-x^n$  is equivalent to  $0$ .
solution_md:
Consider the equivalence relation $\equiv$ on polynomials defined by $p(x) \equiv q(x)$ if the remainders when we divide $p$ and $q$ by $x^6 - x - 1$ are equivalent coefficient-wise modulo 3 (alternatively, we can think of all of our polynomials as having coefficients in the field of integers modulo 3).
Your interpretation must be the correct one,**JBL**; I also disagree with writing $p(\alpha) \equiv q(\alpha) \pmod{3}$ . The polynomial $f(x) = x^6-x-1$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ ; in fact it's even irreducible in $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ . Then $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(f(x))$ is a field, **the** unique finite field $\mathbb{F}_{3^6}$ with $729$ elements, of which elements indeed may be regarded as the classes of equivalence of $0,1,x,\ldots,x^{727}$ , since $\mathbb{F}_{3^6}^*$ is cyclic (this is the thing to which the "it is known ..." refers to). So the problem in effect asks to find the largest $n < 728$ for which the equation $p^3 - p = g^n$ in $p$ has a solution in $\mathbb{F}_{3^6}$ , with $g$ being a generator of $\mathbb{F}_{3^6}^*$ (the condition $n < 728$ being because of course $g^{728} = 1 = g^0$ ). Most likely some Galois theory topic in disguise.

stem_md: Find the maximum of  $x+y$  given that  $x$  and  $y$  are positive real numbers that satisfy \[x^3+y^3+(x+y)^3+36xy=3456.\]
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>We use the standard strategy in these kinds of problems:
Let  $x + y = a$  and  $xy = b$ ,and we want the maximum of  $a$ , so  we have $a(a^2 - 3b) + a^3 + 36b = 3456$  $2a^3 - 3ab + 36b - 3456 = 0$ ,
This is a cubic, so there is no global maximum, but we could get a global maximum on the positive half of the graph. So, we take the derivative. $6a^2 - 3b = 0$ . 
Our possible relative maximums are at  $a = \pm \sqrt{\frac{b}{2}}$  But we choose the positive one. Therefore, we have  $2a^2 = b$ Our new equation is  $2a^3 - 6a^3 + 72a^2 - 3456 =  
-4a^3 + 72a^2 - 3456 = 0$ . Simplifying,  $a^3 - 18a^2 + 864 = 0$ . By rational root theorem, our possible roots could be any divisors of  $864 = 2^5 \times 3^3$ . Checking, we see  $\boxed{12}$  is the maximum.</details>

Note that there are exactly three ways to write the integer  $4$  as a sum of positive odd integers where the order of the summands matters:
\begin{align*}
1+1+1+1&=4,
1+3&=4,
3+1&=4.
\end{align*}
Let  $f(n)$  be the number of ways to write a natural number  $n$  as a sum of positive odd integers where the order of the summands matters.  Find the remainder when  $f(2008)$  is divided by  $100$ .
solution_md:
Sketch SolutionWe have that $f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2)$ so we are finding $F_{2008} \mod 100$ . We’ll proceed using CRT. $F_{2008} \equiv 3 \mod 4$ and $F_{2008} \equiv 21 \mod 25$ . The answer is then $\boxed{71}$ .
May I inquire how you determined the residue of $F_{2008}$ modulo $3$ and $25$ ?
Modulo $4$ has a period of $6$ when dealing with Fibonacci numbers and modulo $25$ has a period of $100$ . Therefore, $F_{2008} \equiv F_4 \equiv 3 \mod 4$ and $F_{2008} \equiv F_8 \equiv 21 \mod 25$ .

stem_md: Arthur stands on a circle drawn with chalk in a parking lot.  It is sunrise and there are birds in the trees nearby.  He stands on one of five triangular nodes that are spaced equally around the circle, wondering if and when the aliens will pick him up and carry him from the node he is standing on.  He flips a fair coin  $12$  times, each time chanting the name of a nearby star system.  Each time he flips a head, he walks around the circle, in the direction he is facing, until he reaches the next node in that direction.  Each time he flips a tail, he reverses direction, then walks around the circle until he reaches the next node in that new direction.  After  $12$  flips, Arthur finds himself on the node at which he started.  He thinks this is fate, but Arthur is quite mistaken.  If  $a$  and  $b$  are relatively prime positive integers such that  $a/b$  is the probability that Arthur flipped exactly  $6$  heads, find  $a+b$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>If I'm not mistaken, this just asking, "What is the probability Arthur gets six heads when he flips a coin  $12$  times?" He has a  $(\frac{1}{2})^6$  chance of getting  $6$  heads, a  $(\frac{1}{2})^6$  chance that the other flips will be tails, and there are  $\binom{12}{6}=924$  ways to arrange the flips. Then the answer is  $(\frac{1}{2})^{12}\cdot \binom{12}{6}=\frac{924}{4096}=\frac{231}{1024}$ .  $a+b=\boxed{1255}$ .</details>

A Pythagorean triple of  $\textit{square numbers}$  is an ordered triple  $(a,b,c)$  such that  $a^2+b^2=c^2$ . Let a Pythagorean triple of  $\textit{triangular numbers}$  (a PTTN) be an ordered triple of positive integers  $(a,b,c)$  such that  $a\leq b<c$  and
\[\dfrac{a(a+1)}2+\dfrac{b(b+1)}2=\dfrac{c(c+1)}2.\]
For instance,  $(3,5,6)$  is a PTTN ( $6+15=21$ ). Here we call both  $a$  and  $b$   $\textit{legs}$  of the PTTN. Find the smallest natural number  $n$  such that  $n$  is a leg of  $\textit{at least}$  six distinct PTTNs.
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution?</summary>We seek to find the smallest integer  $a$  such that there are at least  $6$  distinct solutions to  $$ a^2+a=(c-b)(c+b+1) $$  where we waive the  $a \leq b$  constraint. The left quantity must have at least  $12$  factors for there to exist at least  $6$  distinct pairings of the factors (a pairing. However, we must discard the  $a(a+1)$  pairing, which yields  $b=0$ , so we actually need at least  $7$  distinct pairings and  $14$  factors. A quick check reveals that the first number with at least  $14$  factors of the form  $a^2+a$  is  $14^2+14=210$ , which has  $16$  factors. Here we can explicitly calculate all pairings of  $210$  and get the triples  $(14,104,105),(14,51,53),(14,33,36),(14,18,23),(14,14,20),(11,14,18),(5,14,15)$ , so the answer is  $\boxed{14}$ .</details>

stem_md: Yatta and Yogi play a game in which they begin with a pile of  $n$  stones.  The players take turns removing  $1$ ,  $2$ ,  $3$ ,  $5$ ,  $6$ ,  $7$ , or  $8$  stones from the pile.  That is, when it is a player's turn to remove stones, that player may remove from  $1$  to  $8$  stones, but *cannot* remove exactly  $4$  stones.  The player who removes the last stone *loses*.  Yogi goes first and finds that he has a winning position, meaning that so long as he plays perfectly, Yatta cannot defeat him.  For how many positive integers  $n$  from  $100$  to  $2008$  inclusive is this the case?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Suppose that on Yogi's turn, he removes  $n$  stones from the game. Then Yatta can remove exactly  $9-n$  stones. So Yatta can always force that number down by  $9$ .
This means to win you need the other player to have to move when there are  $9k+1$  stones on the board, for some integer  $k$ .

If  $n\equiv 1,5\pmod{9}$ , then Yatta cannot give Yogi a number that is  $1\pmod 9$ , as he can't play a  $4$  or a  $9$ .

So Yatta will win  $\frac{7}{9}$  of the time. As there are an equal number of each remainders mod 9 from  $101$  to  $2008$ , Yatta will win for  $\frac{7}{9}\cdot 1008=\boxed{784}$   $n$ .  $1001\equiv 1\pmod9$  so we can disregard it.</details>

Given a number  $13k+1$ , we see that the only numbers we can reach are winning by the inductive hypothesis. stem_md: Let  $A$  be the number of  $12$ -digit words that can be formed by from the alphabet  $\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6\}$  if each pair of neighboring digits must differ by exactly  $1$ .  Find the remainder when  $A$  is divided by  $2008$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $m_n$  be the number of  $n$  digit words that end with the digit 3. Likewise, let  $s_n$ ,  $c_n$ , and  $d_n$  be the number of  $n$  digit words that end with the digit 2, 1, and 0, respectively. Note that the number of  $n$  digit words that end with the digit 2 is the same as the number of  $n$  digit words that end with the digit 4, and so on for each of  $c_n$  and  $d_n$ . Then we have   $$ A_n=m_n+2s_n+2c_n+2d_n $$   and we can write the recurrences 
\begin{align*}
m_n &= 2s_{n-1}, 
s_n &= m_{n-1}+c_{n-1}, 
c_n &= s_{n-1}+d_{n-1}, 
d_n &= c_{n-1}.
\end{align*}
With a little substitution we have the recurrence
\begin{align*}
s_n &= 2s_{n-2}+c_{n-1}, 
c_n &= s_{n-1}+c_{n-2}.
\end{align*}
Solving for  $c_n$ , we have that   $$ c_n=4c_{n-2}-2c_{n-4}, $$   so crunching numbers all the way to  $n=12$ , we find that  $A_n=1776+2(1256+1748+724)=9232$ , which leaves a remainder of  $\boxed{1200}$  when divided by 2008.</details>

So do you mean writing for example  $\overline{abc}$  as  $\overline{abcabc}$ ?

Assuming so, let  $N$  have  $d$  digits. Then our number becomes  $N(10^d+1).$ We see 1 digit numbers clearly don't work. In general, we want  $10^d+1$  to not be prime. Odd  $d$  clearly work as  $10+1|10^d+1$  for odd  $d.$ So we set  $d=3,$  which becomes  $1001N=11\cdot 101 \cdot N.$  We want 1)  $N$  to be divisible by  $1001$  and 2)  $N$  to be three digit. This is  $10^{11}+1$  which is divisible by  $11^2.$  To get rid of the other stuff....  $N=(10^{11}+1)/121.$  This is actually fairly easy to find, mod 1000 this becomes  $1/121.$  I won't get into details but after calculation  $1/121$  is  $281$  mod 1000 so our answer is 281 if I didn't make a huge mistake.

stem_md: Let \[X = \cos\frac{2\pi}7 + \cos\frac{4\pi}7 + \cos\frac{6\pi}7 + \cdots + \cos\frac{2006\pi}7 + \cos\frac{2008\pi}7.\] Compute  $\Big|\lfloor 2008 X\rfloor\Big|$ .
solution_md:
Note that any seven consecutive terms are real parts of all of the  $7$ th roots of unity, and therefore must add to  $0$ .

Thus Letting  $\omega=\text{cis }\frac{2\pi}{7}$ , the whole sum just equals  $\cos\frac{2\pi}7 + \cos\frac{4\pi}7 + \cos\frac{6\pi}7=\frac{(\omega+\omega^6)+(\omega^2+\omega^5)+(\omega^3+\omega^4)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\omega^7-1}{\omega-1}-1\right)=-\frac{1}{2}$ .

Finally, plug it in to get  $1004$  for the answer.

stem_md: Find  $k$  where  $2^k$  is the largest power of  $2$  that divides the product \[2008\cdot 2009\cdot 2010\cdots 4014.\]
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The number is  $\frac{4014!}{2007!}$ .

The exponent of the largest power of  $2$  that divides  $4014!$  is  $\lfloor \frac{4014}{2} \rfloor + \lfloor \frac{4014}{2^2} \rfloor + ...$ , which is  $2007 + 1003 + 501 + ...$ .  Stop there; I promise you something cool will happen if you're lazy like me.

The exponent of the largest power of  $2$  that divides  $2007!$  is  $1003 + 501 + ...$  - aha!  Do you see the cool thing that just happened?

We want to subtract the second sum from the first to get the number of factors of  $2$  in  $\frac{4014!}{2007!}$ .  Everything cancels except for the first term in the first sum!  So, the answer is  $\boxed{2007}$ .

Note:  The floor formula comes from counting all numbers that are divisible by  $2$ .  That counts  $2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 ...$  one time each.  But  $4$  donates two factors.  So we add in all numbers divisible by  $4$ :   $4 \cdot 8 \cdot 12 \cdot ...$ .  That takes care of two factors of  $2$  in all those numbers - but  $8$  has three!  So we count  $8 \cdot 16 \cdot 24 \cdot ...$  a third time.  Shower, rinse, repeat.</details>

This solution is a good example of why mathematics exists:  laziness.  Do you really want to add  $12 + 12 + 12 + 12 + ... + 12$ , with the sum containing  $1438$  groups of  $12$ ?  Or would you rather just add  $1438$  groups of  $10$ , and then add  $1438$  groups of  $2$ ?  And then the second part gets broken down even more....

In other words, don't use an axe to break a door.  Just jiggle the key a little!

Let \[\begin{array}{ccccccccccc}A&=&5\cdot 6&-&6\cdot 7&+&7\cdot 8&-&\cdots&+&2003\cdot 2004,B&=&1\cdot 10&-&2\cdot 11&+&3\cdot 12&-&\cdots&+&1999\cdot 2008.\end{array}\] 
Find the value of  $A-B$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The  $n$ th term of  $A$  is  $(n+4)(n+5) = n^2 + 9n + 20$ .

The  $n$ th term of  $B$  is  $n(n+9) = n^2 + 9n$ The  $n$ th term in  $A - B$  is  $(n^2 + 9n + 20) - (n^2 + 9n) = 20$ , with the sign depending on the sign in the original sums.

Thus,  $A - B = 20 - 20 + 20 - 20 + .... + 20$ .

The really cool thing is you don't have to really pay attention to fenceposts that much.  The first and second terms will cancel each other out, since it's  $20 - 20$ .  So, as long as the problem writer is honest, and that last term is a  $+$  (which s/he is, since all the odd-times-even terms have a  $+$ , while the even-times-odds have a  $-$ ), all the terms before the last term will cancel each other out, leaving only a single  $\boxed{20}$  at the end.</details>

stem_md: Simon and Garfunkle play in a round-robin golf tournament. Each player is awarded one point for a victory, a half point for a tie, and no points for a loss. Simon beat Garfunkle in the ﬁrst game by a record margin as Garfunkle sent a shot over the bridge and into troubled waters on the ﬁnal hole. Garfunkle went on to score  $8$  total victories, but no ties at all. Meanwhile, Simon wound up with exactly  $8$  points, including the point for a victory over Garfunkle. Amazingly, every other player at the tournament scored exactly  $n$ . Find the sum of all possible values of  $n$ .
solution_md:
Very very irrelevant but I believe it's spelled Garfunkel.

I'm going to assume yes and try this solution: 
1 point in total is awarded for each match played. There are T(T-1)/2 matches where T is the number of players including Simon and Garfunkel. Simon scores 8 points, Garfunkel scores 8 points, and the rest of the T players (a total of T-2) score n(T-2) points.  $16 + n(T-2) = T(T-1)/2$  Quadratic in T:  $T^2 + (3-2n)T -32=0 $  $(3-2n)^2 + 128 = k^2$  where k is an integer.  $(k+2n-3)(k+3-2n) = 128.$  Do casework on the factors of 128, you'll only get 3 cases. You find k=33, n=17, and T = 33 players including simon and garfunkel. The other cases fail because you get half a player.

stem_md: For how many integers  $1\leq n\leq 9999$  is there a solution to the congruence \[\phi(n)\equiv 2\,\,\,\pmod{12},\] where  $\phi(n)$  is the Euler phi-function?
solution_md:
Suppose  $n = p^k$  for some positive integer  $k$  and  $p > 3$  where  $p$  is a prime number. Thus,  $\phi(n) = p^{k-1}(p-1) \equiv 2 \pmod{12}$ . Since  $\gcd{(p, 12)} = 1$ , we can only have  $p \equiv 1, 5, 7, 11 \pmod{12}$ . If  $p \equiv 1$ , we'd have  $0 \equiv 2 \pmod{12}$ , no solution. If  $p \equiv 5$ , then  $5^{k-1}(4) \equiv 2 \pmod{12}$ , no solution, because the RHS isn't divisible by  $4$ . If  $p \equiv 7 \pmod{12}$ , then the LHS is divisible by  $6$ , but not the RHS. Hence, we must have  $p \equiv 11$ . This would give us  $11^{k-1}(10) \equiv 2 \pmod{12}$ , which reduces to  $(-1)^{k-1} \equiv -1 \pmod{6}$ , which implies that  $k$  is even. 

We must have  $p < 100$  because  $p^2 \le 9999 < 10000$ . The primes congruent to  $11$  modulo  $12$  are:  $11, 23, 47, 59, 71, 83$ , so  $11^2, 23^2, 47^2, 59^2, 71^2, 83^2$  are solutions. But  $11^4 > 10^4 = 10000 > 9999$ , so we can't have  $k > 2$ . 

Now let us consider when  $p = 2$ : we have  $\phi(2^k) = 2^{k-1}$  so we have  $2^{k-1} \equiv 2 \pmod{12}$ , implying that  $k = 2$  is the only solution (otherwise  $4$  divides the LHS and not the RHS). So we have  $2^2 = 4$  is a solution. 

For  $p = 3$ : we have  $\phi(3^k) = 3^{k-1} \cdot 2$  so  $3^{k-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{6}$ , implying that  $k = 1$  is the only solution, giving us  $3$  as a solution. 

So now what if  $n$  is divisible by multiple primes? Say,  $n = p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$ . Then, the totient of this would be  $\text{stuff}(p_1 - 1)(p_2-1)(p_3-1) \cdots$  which is divisible by  $4$ , so the congruence clearly has no solution there. UNLESS...that other prime is  $2$ . 

In conclusion, our solutions are  $3, 4, 11^2, 23^2, 47^2, 59^2, 71^2, 83^2, 2 \cdot 3, 2\cdot 11^2, 2\cdot 23^2, 2\cdot 47^2, 2\cdot 59^2, 2\cdot 71^2, 2\cdot 83^2$  and it is up to the reader to figure out from here how many solutions there are. XD

Click to expand$\begin{cases} x^5+y^5=1x^6+y^6=1\end{cases}$ From the second equa. it can be derived that $\mid x \mid\le1,\mid y \mid\le1$ In the light of this finding, it follows from the first equa. that none of $x, y$ can be negative . If both $<0$ , then $LHS<0 \neq RHS>0$ ; if one of $x,y<0$ , then the other would be $>1$ , since $(-\alpha)^5+\beta^5 = 1 \Rightarrow \beta^5=1+\alpha^5$ $\Rightarrow \beta>1$ . In conclusion, the following constraints arise in the system of equa.: $0\le x\le 1, 0\le y\le 1$ Combining both equa. $\Rightarrow x^5+y^5=x^6+y^6$ . However, within the intervals $0< x< 1, 0< y< 1, x^5+y^5>x^6+y^6$ Equality only occurs at the extremities of the intervals $0\le x\le 1, 0\le y\le 1$ and the only solutions are the trivial ones $(x,y)=(1,0), (0,1)$ .
'Elaboration'To find all the solutions of (x, y) between [0, 1], we have the following: Let $f(x)=x^6-x^5$ . \begin{align*} x^5+y^5&=x^6+y^6 x^5-x^6 &=y^6-y^5 -f(x)&=f(y) \end{align*} However, $f(x)=x^6-x^5 = x^5(x-1)$ . In the interval (0, 1), $x^5$ is positive but $x-1$ is negative, which means $f(x)$ is negative. Then at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ , $f(x) = 0$ .The only possibility of $-f(x)=f(y)$ is that $x$ and $y$ are both $0$ or $1$ , $4$ possibilities. Checking them yields the two valid ones.

Today was the 5th Kettering Olympiad - and here are the problems, which are very good intermediate problems.

1. Find all real  $x$  so that  $(1+x^2)(1+x^4)=4x^3$ 

2. Mark and John play a game. They have  $100$  pebbles on a table. They take turns taking at least one at at most eight pebbles away. The person to claim the last pebble wins. Mark goes first. Can you find a way for Mark to always win? What about John?

3. Prove that
 $\sin x + \sin 3x + \sin 5x + ... + \sin 11 x = (1-\cos 12 x)/(2 \sin x)$ 

4. Mark has  $7$  pieces of paper. He takes some of them and splits each into  $7$  pieces of paper. He repeats this process some number of times. He then tells John he has  $2000$  pieces of paper. John tells him he is wrong. Why is John right?

5. In a triangle  $ABC$ , the altitude, angle bisector, and median split angle  $A$  into four equal angles. Find the angles of  $ABC.$ 

6. There are  $100$  cities. There exist airlines connecting pairs of cities. 

a) Find the minimal number of airlines such that with at most  $k$  plane changes, one can go from any city to any other city.

b) Given that there are  $4852$  airlines, show that, given any schematic, one can go from any city to any other city.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Problem 1</summary>$(1+x^2)(1+x^4)=4x^3$ Since the left hand side must be positive,  $x^3>0$ . $1+x^2+x^4+x^6=4x^3$  $\frac{1}{x^3}+\frac{1}{x}+x+x^3=4$  $\left(\frac{1}{x^3}+x^3\right)+\left(\frac{1}{x}+x\right)=4$ Let  $y=\frac{1}{x}+x$ .
Then  $y^3=\frac{1}{x^3}+\frac{3}{x}+3x+x^3$ . $(y^3-3y)+(y)=4$  $y^3-2y-4=0$ I don't know the method for depressed cubics, so must resort to guess and check. (Good thing  $y=2$  gives a root) $(y-2)(y^2+2y+2)=0$  $y-2$  then  $y=2$ Or  $(y^2+2y+2)=0$  then  $y=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{2^2-4(1)(2)}}{2(1)}$ Since the latter produces imaginary roots, the only possibility is  $y=2$ . $2=\frac{1}{x}+x$ . $x^2-2x+1=(x-1)^2=0$ So  $x=1$  is the only solution.</details>

**p1.** An evil galactic empire is attacking the planet Naboo with numerous automatic drones. The fleet defending the planet consists of  $101$  ships. By the decision of the commander of the fleet, some of these ships will be used as destroyers equipped with one rocket each or as rocket carriers that will supply destroyers with rockets. Destroyers can shoot rockets so that every rocket destroys one drone. During the attack each carrier will have enough time to provide each destroyer with one rocket but not more. How many destroyers and how many carriers should the commander assign to destroy the maximal number of drones and what is the maximal number of drones that the fleet can destroy?**p2.** Solve the inequality:  $\sqrt{x^2-3x+2} \le \sqrt{x+7}$ **p3.** Find all positive real numbers  $x$  and  $y$  that satisfy the following system of equations:  $$ x^y = y^{x-y} $$    $$ x^x = y^{12y} $$  **p4.** A convex quadrilateral  $ABCD$  with sides  $AB = 2$ ,  $BC = 8$ ,  $CD = 6$ , and  $DA = 7$  is divided by a diagonal  $AC$  into two triangles. A circle is inscribed in each of the obtained two triangles. These circles touch the diagonal at points  $E$  and  $F$ . Find the distance between the points  $E$  and  $F$ .**p5.** Find all positive integer solutions  $n$  and  $k$  of the following equation:  $$ \underbrace{11... 1}_{n} \underbrace{00... 0}_{2n+3} + \underbrace{77...7}_{n+1} \underbrace{00...0}_{n+1}+\underbrace{11...1}_{n+2} = 3k^3. $$  **p6.** The Royal Council of the planet Naboo consists of  $12$  members. Some of these members mutually dislike each other. However, each member of the Council dislikes less than half of the members. The Council holds meetings around the round table. Queen Amidala knows about the relationship between the members so she tries to arrange their seats so that the members that dislike each other are not seated next to each other. But she does not know whether it is possible. Can you help the Queen in arranging the seats? Justify your answer.

solution_md: <details><summary>s2</summary>Note that in order for the inequality to be satisfied, we must have that  $x+7\ge x^2-3x+2$ , but note that in the range  $(1,2)$  the LHS factors as  $(x-2)(x-1)$  and thus the expression will result in a negative inside of a square root which would be nonreal. Now, we can rearrange our new inequality to get  $x^2-4x-5\le0$ , or  $(x-5)(x+1)\le0$ . Thus  $x$  must be in the range  $[-1, 5]$ . Taking out the  $(1,2)$  range gives us the solution  $[-1, 1] \cup [2,5]$ .</details>

Since each carrier can supply each destroyer once, our destroyers will have  $1+101-n=102-n$  rockets each (an additional 1 because they carry 1 to begin with). Thus we want to maximize  $n(102-n)$ . Note that the product of two numbers that sum to the same number is largest when the 2 numbers are equal because of difference of squares:  $(n-m)(n+m)=n^2-m^2$  so only when  $m=0$  is  $n^2-m^2$  minimized. Thus we want  $n=51$ , which will destroy  $52^2=2601$  drones.</details>

<details><summary>S4</summary>Let  $a$  be the side length of the equilateral triangle, and  $h$  be the altitude (height).
Let  $d_1, d_2, d_3$  be the shortest distances from Captain America's location to the three roads.  $$ \frac {1}{2}a(d_1+ d_2+ d_3) = \frac {1}{2}ah $$    $$ \implies h=d_1+ d_2+ d_3=50 $$    $$ \implies a=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}h=\boxed {\frac {100\sqrt{3}}{3}} $$</details>

stem_md:
We say that an integer  $a$  is a quadratic, cubic, or quintic residue modulo  $n$  if there exists an integer  $x$  such that  $x^2\equiv a \pmod n$ ,  $x^3 \equiv a \pmod n$ , or  $x^5 \equiv a \pmod n$ , respectively. Further, an integer  $a$  is a primitive residue modulo  $n$  if it is exactly one of these three types of residues modulo  $n$ .

How many integers  $1 \le a \le 2015$  are primitive residues modulo  $2015$ ?

*Proposed by Michael Ren*
solution_md:
Ok, since I guess this is indeed the intended solution, I'll fill in the aforementioned details.

Let's first find the number of quadratic residues. As per the lemma, there are 3 residues modulo 5, 7 modulo 13, and 16 modulo 31; therefore, by CRT there are  $3 \cdot 7 \cdot 16=336$  quadratic residues modulo 2015. Now we need to find the number of cubic residues: by the same lemma, there are 5 cubic residues modulo 5, 5 modulo 13, and 11 modulo 31; therefore, by CRT, there are  $5 \cdot 5 \cdot 11=275$  cubic residues modulo 2015. Finally, there are 5 fifth residues modulo 5, 13 modulo 13, and 7 modulo 31, so there are  $5 \cdot 13 \cdot 7=455$  fifth residues modulo 2015.

Now we move on to 6th residues; i.e. both quadratic and cubic residues. Per the lemma there are 3 of these modulo 5, 3 modulo 13, and 6 modulo 31, for a total of 54 modulo 2015. Continuing, there are 3 tenth residues modulo 5, 7 modulo 13, and 4 modulo 31, so there are 84 tenth residues modulo 2015. Finally, there are 5 fifteenth residues modulo 5, 5 modulo 13, and 3 modulo 31, so there are 75 modulo 2015.

Lastly, there are 3 30th residues modulo 5, 3 modulo 13, and 2 modulo 31, so there are 18 30th residues modulo 2015.

We want to count the residues that are **exactly** one of quadratic, cubic, or fifth, so by PIE our answer is  $336+275+455-2(54+84+75)+3(18)=\boxed{694}$  (to check: each primitive residue is counted once, sixth/tenth/fifteenth residues are counted  $1+1-2(1)=0$  times, and 30th residues are counted  $1+1+1-2(1+1+1)+3(1)=0$  times like we want).

\begin{align*}
h^2+k^2&=x^2 
h^2+k^2-2k\sqrt{2}+2&=y^2
\end{align*}
Subtracting the two, we get  $x^2-y^2=2k\sqrt{2}-2=\sqrt{5}$ , so  $k=\frac{\sqrt{5}+2}{2\sqrt{2}}$ .

Now here we might notice a potential issue: namely,  $k>\sqrt{2}$ , so the triangle we're talking about doesn't actually exist. But fortunately we don't actually care at all because all these things are polynomial identities (this is the same reason that 2014 HMMT Algebra #9 can be solved geometrically despite involving complex numbers).

Moving on, let's discover some more things about our nonexistent triangle! For example, let's find the area, which is both  $\frac{1}{2}xy\sin 120^{\circ}=\frac{xy\sqrt{3}}{4}$  and  $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot h$ ; ergo  $xy\sqrt{3}=2h\sqrt{2}$ , or  $3x^2y^2=8h^2$ . Now we fill in  $y^2=x^2-\sqrt{5}$  and  $h^2=x^2-\frac{9+4\sqrt{5}}{8}$  to get
\begin{align*}
3(x^2-\sqrt{5})x^2&=8\left(x^2-\frac{9+4\sqrt{5}}{8}\right) 
3(x^2-\sqrt{5})x^2&=8x^2-(9+4\sqrt{5}) 
3x^4-x^2(3\sqrt{5}+8)+(9+4\sqrt{5})&=0 
x^2&=\frac{3\sqrt{5}+8+\sqrt{(109+48\sqrt{5})-(108+48\sqrt{5})}}{6} 
x^2&=\frac{3\sqrt{5}+8 \pm 1}{6}
\end{align*}
Thus we have  $$ x^2=\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{3\sqrt{5}+7}{6} $$  which leads to  $x=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$  or  $\frac{3\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{15}}{6}$  (that second one comes from being like "hm, how do we get this thing squared; let's try squaring  $3+\sqrt{5}$  oh darn we're off by a factor of  $\sqrt{12}$ ), whose sum is  $$ \sum x=\frac{3+3\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{15}}{6} $$  or  $\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}}+\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{12}}$ , making the  $\sum a_i=\frac{8}{3}$ , and the answer is  $\boxed{803}$ .</details>

What is the largest positive integer which is equal to the sum of its digits?

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md: First, notice that any one-digit integer is equal to the sum of its digits, and  $9$  is the largest one digit number. Now suppose there were a two-digit number  $AB$ , where  $A$  and  $B$  are digits, that was equal to the sum of its digits. We would have the equation  $10A+B=A+B \implies A=0$ . Thus, the largest possible integer equal to the sum of its digits is the largest one-digit number, or  $\boxed{9}$ .

For every student  $S$ , we define his or her *ratio* to be the number of students of the opposite gender as  $S$  divided by the number of students of the same gender as  $S$  (including  $S$ ). Let  $ABC$  be an isosceles triangle with  $\angle A = 90^{\circ}$ . Points  $D$  and  $E$  are selected on sides  $AB$  and  $AC$ , and points  $X$  and  $Y$  are the feet of the altitudes from  $D$  and  $E$  to side  $BC$ .  Given that  $AD = 48\sqrt2$  and  $AE = 52\sqrt2$ , compute  $XY$ .

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md: **Solution:** Let  $AB = BC = x$ . By similar triangles, we have that  $DX = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{48\sqrt{2}}{x} \cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} = BX$ . Similarly,  $EY = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{52\sqrt{2}}{x} \cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} = CY$ . Notice that  $XY = BC - (BX + CY) = x\sqrt{2} - \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \left(2 - \frac{100\sqrt{2}}{x}\right)$   $= x\sqrt{2} - x\sqrt{2} + \frac{100\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = \boxed{100}$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/Online Math Open Problems/2015 Online Math Open Problems/1077898.json

stem_md:
We delete the four corners of a  $8 \times 8$  chessboard. How many ways are there to place eight non-attacking rooks on the remaining squares?

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md: **Solution:** Label the columns of the chessboard  $1$  through  $8$ , from left to right. Notice that there must be exactly one rook on each of these columns. There are  $2 \cdot \binom{6}{2}$  ways to place the two rooks in columns  $1$  and  $8$ . Now, note that for the rooks in column  $2$  through  $7$ , there are simply  $6!$  ways to arrange those. Hence, our answer is  $2 \cdot \binom{6}{2} \cdot 6! = \boxed{21600}$ .

Let  $ABC$  be a scalene triangle whose side lengths are positive integers. It is called *stable* if its three side lengths are multiples of 5, 80, and 112, respectively. What is the smallest possible side length that can appear in any stable triangle?

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md: Let the length of the sides of the triangle denote  $50a, 80b, 112c$ . Evidently, the smallest possible side length must be the side length of multiple of  $5$ . By Triangle Inequality:   $$ 5a + 112c > 80b $$     $$ 5a + 80b > 112c $$     $$ \implies 5a > |80b-112c| = 16|5b-7c| $$   Since  $\gcd(5, 7) = 1$ , by Bezout's Lemma, there exists  $(b, c) = (b_0, c_0)$  such that:   $$ 5b_0-7c_0 = 1 $$   Hence  $5a > 16$  or  $5a \ge 20$ . The smallest possible value is  $\boxed{20}$

stem_md:
Let  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ , and  $d$  be positive real numbers such that
\[a^2 + b^2 - c^2 - d^2 = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad a^2 - b^2 - c^2 + d^2 = \frac{56}{53}(bc + ad).\]
Let  $M$  be the maximum possible value of  $\tfrac{ab+cd}{bc+ad}$ . If  $M$  can be expressed as  $\tfrac{m}{n}$ , where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers, find  $100m + n$ .

*Proposed by Robin Park*
solution_md:
The first equation implies the existence of  $r, x, y$  with \[\begin{cases}a=r\sin x  b=r\cos x c=r\sin y d=r\cos y\end{cases}\] and the second, following this substitution, is equivalent to \[\cos 2y - \cos 2x = \frac{56}{53}\cdot \sin(x+y).\]

Since  $\cos 2y - \cos 2x = 2\sin(x+y)\sin(x-y)$ , we get that  $\sin(x-y) = \frac{28}{53}\Longrightarrow \cos(x-y) = \frac{45}{53}$ . 

The expression we are asked to maximize is \[\frac{\sin 2x + \sin 2y}{2\sin(x+y)} = \frac{2\sin(x+y)\cos(x-y)}{2\sin(x+y)} = \cos(x-y) = \frac{45}{53},\] so our answer is just  $4553.\;\blacksquare$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/Online Math Open Problems/2015 Online Math Open Problems/1077911.json

stem_md:
Joe is given a permutation  $p = (a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4, a_{5})$  of  $(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)$ . A *swap* is an ordered pair  $(i, j)$  with  $1 \le i < j \le 5$ , and this allows Joe to swap the positions  $i$  and  $j$  in the permutation. For example, if Joe starts with the permutation  $(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)$ , and uses the swaps  $(1, 2)$  and  $(1, 3)$ , the permutation becomes
\[(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) \rightarrow (2, 1, 3, 4, 5) \rightarrow (3, 1, 2, 4, 5). \]Out of all  $\tbinom{5}{2} = 10$  swaps, Joe chooses  $4$  of them to be in a set of swaps  $S$ . Joe notices that from  $p$  he could reach any permutation of  $(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)$  using only the swaps in  $S$ . How many different sets are possible?

*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md:
<details><summary>in-depth solution</summary>First, we convert the swaps  $p$  into a graph  $p'$  where a swap  $(i,j)$  connects vertices  $i$  and  $j$ . (The graph has  $5$  vertices). Clearly  $p'$  must be a connected graph. 

Now, we use the well-known lemma that any connected graph of  $n$  vertices and  $n-1$  edges is a tree.  $n=5$  gives that each graph  $p'$  is a tree.

Lemma: All trees work.

Proof: We use induction. First, since the tree is connected, continually swap  $5$  until it reaches its desired position. Then we have a tree on  $4$  vertices, and our inductive hypothesis or whatever takes care of the rest.

Now that any connected tree works, we use the well-known formula that there are  $n^{n-2}$  trees on  $n$  labelled vertices, giving us  $5^3=125$  sets of swaps.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/Online Math Open Problems/2015 Online Math Open Problems/1077912.json

stem_md:
Alex starts with a rooted tree with one vertex (the root). For a vertex  $v$ , let the size of the subtree of  $v$  be  $S(v)$ . Alex plays a game that lasts nine turns. At each turn, he randomly selects a vertex in the tree, and adds a child vertex to that vertex. After nine turns, he has ten total vertices. Alex selects one of these vertices at random (call the vertex  $v_1$ ). The expected value of  $S(v_1)$  is of the form  $\tfrac{m}{n}$  for relatively prime positive integers  $m, n$ . Find  $m+n$ .**Note:** In a rooted tree, the subtree of  $v$  consists of its indirect or direct descendants (including  $v$  itself).

*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>Prove this by induction. If there are  $n$   vertices at the end, then the expected value will be  $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{i}$ .
Obviously, if there is only one point, then the expected size is one, satisfying the condition. 
Let  $E[n]$  be the expected number of vertices whose subtree contains a specific random vertex. This value is easily seen to be the same as the expected size of the subtree of a random vertex.

Now, for the  $n$ th vertex added, the expected size of it's subtree is  $E[n-1]+1$ , as all the subtrees that contain the vertex it is put onto will contain the new vertex, and the subtree rooted at the vertex added will also contain it. Ergo,  $E[n]=\frac{1}{n}(E[n-1]+1)+\frac{n-1}{n}E[n-1]=E[n-1]+\frac{1}{n}$ . This proves the induction.

Ergo, we want  $\sum_{i=1}^{10}\frac{1}{i}=\frac{7381}{2520}$ , so the answer is  $\boxed{9901}$</details>

stem_md:
Consider polynomials  $P$  of degree  $2015$ , all of whose coefficients are in the set  $\{0,1,\dots,2010\}$ . Call such a polynomial *good* if for every integer  $m$ , one of the numbers  $P(m)-20$ ,  $P(m)-15$ ,  $P(m)-1234$  is divisible by  $2011$ , and there exist integers  $m_{20}, m_{15}, m_{1234}$  such that  $P(m_{20})-20, P(m_{15})-15, P(m_{1234})-1234$  are all multiples of  $2011$ . Let  $N$  be the number of good polynomials. Find the remainder when  $N$  is divided by  $1000$ .

*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md:
Throughout the proof, we work over  $\mathbb{F}_{2011}[x]$  (so modulo  $2011$ , which is prime). 

Take  $P(x) = Q(x)\left(x^{2011}-x\right) + R(x)$ , where  $\deg R\le 2010$  and  $\deg Q = 4$ . The values  $R$  takes modulo  $2011$  uniquely define it. Since  $R$  maps  $\mathbb{N}$  to  $\{20, 15, 1234\}$  and is in fact surjective to the latter set, there are  $3^{2011} - 3( 2^{2011} - 2) - 3$  choices for  $R$ . 

Now, the identity of  $Q$  does not affect what  $P$  is modulo  $2011.$  The only condition we need to impose is that the leading coefficient of  $Q$  be nonzero, to ensure that  $\deg P = 2015$ . So there are  $2010 * 2011^4$  choices for  $Q$ . 

Since the independent choices of  $Q$  and  $R$  uniquely define  $P$ , we find that  $N = \left(3^{2011} - 3( 2^{2011} - 2) - 3\right)\cdot 2010 \cdot 2011^4\equiv 460\pmod {1000}.\;\blacksquare$

Let  $N = 12!$  and denote by  $X$  the set of positive divisors of  $N$  other than  $1$ . A *pseudo-ultrafilter*  $U$  is a nonempty subset of  $X$  such that for any  $a,b \in X$ :
\begin{itemize}
\item If  $a$  divides  $b$  and  $a \in U$  then  $b \in U$ .
\item If  $a,b \in U$  then  $\gcd(a,b) \in U$ .
\item If  $a,b \notin U$  then  $\operatorname{lcm} (a,b) \notin U$ .
\end{itemize}
How many such pseudo-ultrafilters are there?

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md: <details><summary>sol</summary>The answer is  $\boxed{19}$ . First prove that the number of pseudo-ultrafilters of  $p^a$  is  $a$ . Then, it is clear that if  $N={p_1}^{a_1}{p_2}^{a_2}..$ , then two different primes (or powers) cannot be in the same set since then the  $\gcd$  of them $=1$  would be in the set which is contradiction. From these two points, it is clear that the answer is the sum of the powers appearing in the prime factorization of  $N$  which gives  $19$  in this case.</details>

stem_md:
Suppose we have  $10$  balls and  $10$  colors. For each ball, we (independently) color it one of the  $10$  colors, then group the balls together by color at the end. If  $S$  is the expected value of the square of the number of distinct colors used on the balls, find the sum of the digits of  $S$  written as a decimal.

*Proposed by Michael Kural*
solution_md:
Interestingly, it seems that everyone has come up with different solutions (and different from how I did it), which I am happy to see.
Here is the official solution:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We solve the problem for the general case of  $n$  balls and  $n$  colors for  $n\ge 2$ .

Let  $C$  be the set of colors, so  $|C|=10$ . Let  $B$  be the set of colors which are the color of some ball, so we want to find  $E[|B|^2]$ .
For a set  $T\subseteq C$ , let  $f(T)$  be the probability that  $B=T$ , and let  $g(T)$  be the probability that  $B\subseteq T$ . So then
\[
E[|B|^2] = \sum_{T\subseteq C} f(T)|T|^2
\]
and also
\[
g(T)=\sum_{R\subseteq T} f(T)
\]
Clearly,  $g(T)=\frac{|T|^n}{n^n}$ . By Mobius Inversion, (this is also essentially Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion; there are a lot of ways to see that this identity holds)
\[
f(T)=\sum_{R \subseteq T} (-1)^{|T|-|R|}g(R)
\]
Thus
\begin{align*}
E[|B|]^2=\sum_{T\subseteq C}\sum_{R\subseteq T} (-1)^{|T|-|R|}g(R)|T|^2&=\sum_{R\subseteq C}\sum_{R\subseteq T\subseteq C} (-1)^{|T|-|R|}g(R)|T|^2
&=\sum_{i = 0}^n\sum_{j=i}^n \binom{n}{i}\binom{n-i}{j-i}(-1)^{j-i}\frac{i^n}{n^n}j^2
\end{align*}
where we set  $i=|R|,j=|T|,$  since there are  $\binom{n}{i}$  choices for  $R$  given fixed  $i$  and  $\binom{n-i}{j-i}$  choices for  $T$  given  $j$  and  $R\subseteq T$ .

Lemma:
If  $x$  is a real number and  $p,q$  are nonnegative integers with  $p>q$ , then
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{p} (-1)^k\binom{p}{k}(x+k)^q=0
\]

Proof:
This is simply saying that the  $p$ th finite difference of a  $q$ th degree polynomial is  $0$ , which is true because each successive finite difference decreases the degree of the polynomial by  $1$ .


Then note that if  $n-i>2$ ,
\[
\sum_{j=i}^n\binom{n-i}{j-i}(-1)^{j-i}j^2=0.
\]
so our expression for  $E[|B|^2]$  simply reduces to
\[
E[|B|^2]=\sum_{i=n-2}^n\sum_{j=i}^n\binom{n}{i}\binom{n-si}{j-i}(-1)^{j-i}\frac{i^n}{n^n}j^2.
\]
Evaluating this sum yields
\[
E[|B|^2]=\binom{n}{n-2}\frac{(n-2)^n}{n^n}\left(n^2-2(n-1)^2+(n-2)^2\right)
\]
\[
+\binom{n}{n-1}\frac{(n-1)^n}{n^n}\left((n-2)^2-(n-1)^2\right)+\binom{n}{n}\frac{n^n}{n^n}\left(n^2\right)
\]
which simplifies to
\[
\frac{1}{n^n}\left(n(n-1)(n-2)^n+n(1-2n)(n-1)^n+n^{n+2}\right)
\]
For  $n=10$ , this is
\[
43.414772797
\]
yielding a final answer of  $\boxed{55}$ .</details>

Alternatively (elaborating on the above post), we may do the following.

Enumerate the  $10^{10}$  coloring states in some order, and define the indicator \[x_{k,j}  = \begin{cases} 1 \text{ if the } j\text{th color is used in the } k\text{th row} 0 \text{ else}\end{cases}\] for  $1\le k\le 10^{10}$  and  $1\le j\le 10$ .

The expected value scaled by  $10^{10}$  (since we only care about the sum of the digits), by definition will be \[S = \sum_{k=1}^{10^{10}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{10}x_{k,j}\right)^2 = \sum_{k=1}^{10^{10}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{10}x_{k,j}^2 +\sum_{1\le i,j\le 10}x_{k,i}x_{k,j}\right).\]

Since  $x_{k,j}^2=x_{k,j}$ , the first summation is just \[\sum_{k=1}^{10^{10}}\sum_{j=1}^{10}x_{k,j}^2 = 10\left(10^{10} - 9^{10}\right),\] because there are  $10$  color choices and each appears in  $10^{10} - 9^{10}$  colorings.

For the second sum, since there are  $\binom{10}{2}$  pairs of colors, and any two colors will simultaneously occur in  $10^{10} - 2 * 9^{10} + 8^{10}$  , we compute \[\sum_{k=1}^{10^{10}}\sum_{1\le i,j\le 10}x_{k,i}x_{k,j} = 2\binom{10}{2}\left(10^{10} - 2 * 9^{10} + 8^{10}\right)\]

Adding these results, we obtain  $S = 43147727970$ , with sum of digits  $55.\;\blacksquare$
