So essentially we're trying to prove that \[ g(T)=\sum_{R\subseteq T} g(R)\Leftrightarrow f(T)\sum_{R\subseteq T} (-1)^{|T|-|R|} g(R) \] This is an important relation in general. I'll explain why this should make sense intuitively, and then I'll give two actual proofs. First, this would be a very familiar kind of relation to those who have worked with Mobius inversion (I have and will continue to omit the umlaut for the sanity of my typing). If you're not interested, you can skip this part, but I think it gives some interesting and useful motivation. In a usual, number theoretic context, [the Mobius inversion formula](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_inversion_formula) refers to the following:
If $f(n)$ is some function on the positive integers, and $g$ is another function defined such that \[ g(n)=\sum_{d\mid n} f(d) \] for all $n$ , then it is also true that \[ f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)g(d) \] where $\mu$ is the [Mobius function](http://mathworld.wolfram.com/MoebiusFunction.html), a certain number theoretic function defined by \[ \mu(n)=\begin{cases} 0\text{ if some }p^2\mid n\text{, }p\text{ prime } (-1)^k\text{ otherwise, }k\text{ the number of prime divisors of }n \end{cases} \]
The Mobius function itself isn't too important in this context, but there are clearly some similarities between this and the thing we're dealing with above. In both cases, we're given $g$ as some function summing $f$ over all subparts (in the OMO problem, this is subsets, and in the number theoretic context, this is divisors). We then backsolve using a similar sum but multiplying by some factor which is sometimes positive and negative (in the first context, this is the $(-1)^{|T|-|R|}$ factor, and in the second, this is $\mu(n/d)$ ). Note also that this factor depends not on the part $R$ or $d$ itself, but on the "difference" between $R$ and $T$ or between $d$ and $n$ , leading to $|T|-|R|$ and $n/d$ . You might be suspcicious that this all isn't just a coincidence, and in fact these are both specific instances of the same general phenomenon: using Mobius inversion on something called an *incidence algebra* on a *poset*. It turns out that $(-1)^{|T|}$ is the Mobius function of a set $T$ in this incidence algebra on sets and subsets, so really $(-1)^{|T|-|R|}$ is $(-1)^{|T-R|}$ in disguise, where $T-R$ is the set of all elements of $T$ not contained in $R$ . This has digressed considerably, but the point is that this provides a lot of motivation for why this stuff actually works out. For a different approach, we are emulating a lot of the same ideas as PIE here, although not in exactly the same way. The idea of PIE is that at each step we make a rough estimate and adjust for error with each successive term. The full statement is \[ |A_1\cup A_2\cup \cdots \cup A_n|=|A_1|+|A_2|+\cdots +|A_n|-|A_1\cap A_2|-\cdots-|A_{n-1}\cap A_n|+\cdots \pm |A_1\cap A_2\cdots A_n| \] When we want to compute $|A_1\cup A_2\cup \cdots A_n|$ , naively we can estimate it with $|A_1|+|A_2|+\cdots + |A_n|$ . However, of course this double counts some elements, so we subtract off some of the overlap with the $|A_i\cap A_j|$ terms. Then we realize that we subtracted off too much of the overlap, so we add back some $|A_i\cap A_j\cap A_k|$ terms, and so on. We go through a similar process trying to backsolve for $f$ . If we want to find $f(T)$ for a given set $T$ but only have subset sums $g$ , the simplest thing that we could do is to use $g(T)$ as an estimate. Of course, this is a really bad approximation-in particular, it counts $f(R)$ for all of the subsets $R$ of $T$ with $|T|-1$ elements. To get rid of these, we subtract off the $g(R)$ s. But then we have too few of the subsets of size $|T|-2$ , so we add them back... etc. We keep carrying out this process and end up with an alternating sum like the one in PIE. So hopefully by now you believe that this identity could be true. In my opinion, the proofs are the least important part here, but if you're interested, here they are. First, we can prove the relation directly from PIE if we're tricky about it. Note that PIE still holds true if we weight the elements and define the size of a subset to be the sum of the weights of these elements. We now let our $A_i$ s be *sets of the subsets of* $T$ *themselves*-the weight of each subsets $R$ is $f(R)$ . So in this context \[ |S|=\sum_{R\in S} f(R) \] Specifically, let $|T|=j$ (the actual size, not the weighted size as we just described) as we do later on in the solution for convenience, and suppose that the elements of $T$ are $1,2,\cdots j$ . Let $B_i=\{1,2,\cdots i-1, i+1,\cdots j\}$ for $1\le i\le j$ , so the $B_i$ correspond to the $j-1$ elements subsets of $T$ . We also let $\mathcal{P}(T)$ denote the power set of $T$ (the set of all subsets of $T$ ). Then we let \[ A_i=\mathcal{P}(B_i)=\{R|R\subseteq B_i\} \] or in other words, the set of all subsets of $B_i$ . What is $A_1\cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_n$ ? Simply the set of all subsets of $T$ other than $T$ itself, since something is in some $A_i$ iff it is a subset of $T$ of size at most $j-1$ . So \[ |A_1\cup A_2\cup \cdots \cup A_n|=\sum_{R\in \mathcal{P}(T), R\neq T} f(R)=-f(T)+\sum_{R\subseteq T} f(R)=-f(T)+g(T) \] What is $\bigcap_{i\in R} A_{i}$ for some subset $R$ of $T$ ? Its elements are just those who are not in $A_i$ for any $A_i$ , so those which do not contain $i$ for any $i\in R$ . In other words, \[ \bigcap_{i\in R} A_i=\mathcal{P}(T-R) \] where $T-R$ is set subtraction as I explained above (the set of all elements of $T$ which are not in $R$ ). Observe then that \[ |\bigcap_{i\in R} A_i| = |\mathcal{P}(T-R)| = g(T-R). \] So now PIE says \[ |A_1\cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_n|=\sum_{R\subseteq T, R\neq \emptyset} (-1)^{|R|+1}|\bigcap_{i\in R} A_i| \] demonstrating, by the above, that \[ -f(T)+g(T)=\sum_{R\subseteq T, R\neq \emptyset} (-1)^{|R|+1}g(T-R) \] If we let $S=T-R$ in the righthand set, the above rearranges to \[ -f(T)+g(T)=\sum_{S\subseteq T, S\neq T} (-1)^{|T|-|S|+1}g(S) \] so \[ f(T)=g(T)+\sum_{S\subseteq T, S\neq T} (-1)^{|T|-|S|}g(S)=\sum_{S\subseteq T} (-1)^{|T|-|S|}g(S) \] as desired. We can also prove it directly in an algebraic way. The steps we go through here will be pretty similar to how we actually finish the problem itself. We want to prove the identity \[ f(T)=\sum_{R\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|R|}g(R)=\sum_{R\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|R|} \sum_{S\subseteq R} (-1)^{|T|-|R|} f(S) \] For each $S\subseteq T$ , we count the coefficient of $f(S)$ on the right hand side. If $S=T$ , clearly this is $1$ , as $f(T)$ only shows up once in the case $S=R=T$ with coefficient $(-1)^{|T|-|T|}=1$ . Otherwise, suppose $S\neq T$ . We aim to show that $\sum_{S\subseteq R\subseteq T} (-1)^{|T|-|R|}=0$ , where we are summing over $R$ . Since $T$ is fixed, it suffices to show \[ \sum_{S\subseteq R\subseteq T} (-1)^{R}=0 \] In the context of incidence algebras, as we referenced above, this sum of all $R$ "between" $S$ and $T$ is the sum over an *interval*, which we want to show is $0$ if the interval is nontrivial. Suppose that there are $k$ elements of $T$ which are not elements of $S$ . The simplest expression containing  $f(1,2,3)$  is
\[
g(1,2,3)=f(1,2,3)+f(1,2)+f(2,3)+f(3,1)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f()
\]
but now we have extra factors on the right hand side. We continue trying to eliminate the "biggest" sets that we don't actually want, so in particular we try to eliminate  $f(1,2),f(2,3),f(3,1)$  now. Note that  $g(1,2)=f(1,2)+f(1)+f(2)+f()$ , so subtracting off  $g(1,2),g(2,3),g(3,1)$  from the left hand side and canelling yields
\[
g(1,2,3)-g(1,2)-g(2,3)-g(3,1)=f(1,2,3)-f(1)-f(2)-f(3)-2f()
\]
Now we want to get rid of the  $f(1),f(2),f(3)$ , so we add back  $g(1),g(2),g(3)$  to get
\[
g(1,2,3)-g(1,2)-g(2,3)-g(3,1)+g(1)+g(2)+g(3)=f(1,2,3)+f()
\]
and now we can finally subtract off  $g()=f()$  from both sides, miraculously yielding
\[
g(1,2,3)-g(1,2)-g(2,3)-g(3,1)+g(1)+g(2)+g(3)-g()=f(1,2,3)
\]
This process doesn't prove anything, but it should hopefully convince you that if we successively "fix" the biggest sets on the right hand side by cancelling them out with corresponding  $g(\text{something})$ s,  we get some kind of alternating some of  $g(\text{something})$ s by the end of the process on the left hand side.

Let  $V_0 = \varnothing$  be the empty set and recursively define  $V_{n+1}$  to be the set of all  $2^{|V_n|}$  subsets of  $V_n$  for each  $n=0,1,\dots$ . For example \[
	V_2 = \left\{ \varnothing, \left\{ \varnothing \right\} \right\}
	\quad\text{and}\quad
	V_3 
	=
	\left\{ 
	  \varnothing,
	  \left\{ \varnothing \right\},
	  \left\{ \left\{ \varnothing \right\} \right\},
	  \left\{ \varnothing, \left\{ \varnothing \right\} \right\}
	\right\}.
\] A set  $x \in V_5$  is called *transitive* if each element of  $x$  is a subset of  $x$ . How many such transitive sets are there?

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md:
Here's my solution. It's sort of caseworky, but it's not that bad.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Rather than deal directly with  $V_5,$  which has  $2^{|V_4|} = 2^{2^{|V_3|}} = 2^{2^4} = 65536$  elements, note that  $V_5$  is defined as the set of all subsets of  $V_4$  (the *power set* of  $V_4$ ). Hence  $x \in V_5 \iff x \subseteq V_4.$  That is, we instead consider the subsets of  $V_4.$ Let the elements of  $V_3$  be  $A = \varnothing,$   $B = \{\varnothing\},$   $C = \{\{\varnothing\}\},$  and  $D = \{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}.$  Note that  $B = \{A\},$   $C = \{B\},$  and  $D = \{A, B\}.$  Then \[\begin{aligned} V_4 &= \left\{\,\varnothing = A, \right.  &\qquad\{A\} = B, \{B\} = C, \{C\}, \{D\},  &\qquad \{A, B\} = D, \{A, C\}, \{A, D\}, \{B, C\}, \{B, D\}, \{C, D\},  &\qquad \{A, B, C\}, \{A, B, D\}, \{A, C, D\}, \{B, C, D\},  &\qquad \left.\{A, B, C, D\}\,\right\}. \end{aligned}\] Suppose that  $x$  is a subset of  $V_4.$  Each element of  $x$  is a subset of  $x,$  so if  $u \in x,$  then all of the elements of  $u$  are also in  $x.$  (For example, if  $\{A, B, D\} \in x,$  then we must have  $A, B, D \in X$  as well.) Therefore, we take cases on which of  $A, B, C, D$  we include in  $x,$  which gives certain restrictions on which other elements of  $V_4$  we can include in  $x.$ To speed this up, note that  $B = \{A\}$  implies that if  $B \in x,$  then  $A \in x$  also, so we can exclude any combination of  $A, B, C, D$  where  $B \in x$  but  $A \not\in x.$  Similarly, since  $C = \{B\},$  we must have  $B \in x$  if  $C \in x,$  so if  $C \in x,$  then \textit{both}  $A, B \in x.$  Finally, if  $D \in x,$  then both  $A, B \in x$  as well. In summary,  $A$  is required for each of  $B, C, D$  to be in  $x,$  and  $B$  is required for each of  $C, D$  to be in  $x.$ Then the possible combinations of  $A, B, C, D$  in  $x$  are 

- None of them. This gives just one set,  $x = \varnothing,$  as none of the other  $12$  elements of  $V_4$  can be in  $x.$
- Just  $A.$  This gives just the set  $x = \{A\},$  as no sets besides  $A, B, C, D$  have only the requirement that  $A$  is included.
- Just  $A$  and  $B.$  This gives just the set  $x = \{A, B\},$  as no sets besides  $A, B, C, D$  have only the requirement that  $A$  and/or  $B$  is included.
- Just  $A, B, C.$  Then we can include the four other sets  $\{C\},$   $\{A, C\},$   $\{B, C\},$  and  $\{A, B, C\}$  in  $x.$  Therefore, we get  $2^4 = 16$  sets here.
- Just  $A, B, D.$  Here we can include  $\{D\},$   $\{A, D\},$   $\{B, D\},$  and  $\{A, B, D\},$  so we get  $2^4 = 14$  sets as well.
- All four of  $A, B, C, D.$  Here we can include any of the other twelve sets, so we get  $2^{12} = 4096$  possible sets.
 In total, there are  $1 + 1 + 1 + 16 + 16 + 4096 = \boxed{4131}$  possible sets  $x.$   $\square$</details>

stem_md:
Consider a sequence  $T_0, T_1, \dots$  of polynomials defined recursively by  $T_0(x) = 2$ ,  $T_1(x)=x$ , and  $T_{n+2}(x) = xT_{n+1}(x) - T_n(x)$  for each nonnegative integer  $n$ .  Let  $L_n$  be the sequence of Lucas Numbers, defined by  $L_0 = 2$ ,  $L_1 = 1$ , and  $L_{n+2} = L_n+L_{n+1}$  for every nonnegative integer  $n$ . 

Find the remainder when  $ T_0\left( L_0 \right) + T_1 \left( L_2 \right) + T_2 \left( L_4 \right) + \dots + T_{359} \left( L_{718} \right)$  is divided by  $359$ .

*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md: By induction, if  $T_1(x)=\omega+\tfrac{1}{\omega}$ , then  $T_k=\omega^k+\tfrac{1}{\omega^k}$ . Since  $L_k = \phi ^k + \tfrac{1}{\phi^k}$ ,  $T_k(L_{2k})=\phi^{2k^2}+\tfrac{1}{\phi^{2k^2}}$ . We're summing this from  $k=0$  to  $k=359$  and we want it mod 359. Since  $359\equiv 4\mod 5$ ,  $5$  is a quadratic residue mod 359. So  $\phi$  is some guy mod 359. The order of  $\phi^2$  divides  $179$  and it's not  $1$ , so it's  $179$ . Let  $\phi^2 = x$ . Since  $179\equiv 3\mod 4$ ,  $-1$  is not a quadratic residue mod 179. Now consider the two lists of integers  $x^{1^2}$ ,  $x^{2^2}$ , ...,  $x^{79^2}$  and  $x^{-1^2}$ ,  $x^{-2^2}$ , ...,  $x^{-79^2}$ . No two integers from the same list are the same mod 359 because the order of  $x$  is  $179$ , and no two integers from different lists are the same mod 359 because  $-1$  is not a quadratic residue mod 179. There are  $178$  integers in the list, and they're all distinct mod 359. So they're  $x, x^2, x^3, ..., x^{178}$  in some order. Use the geometric series formula to compute their sum. A bunch of stuff cancels, and you end up with  $2+x+\tfrac{1}{x}=2+3=\boxed{5}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ABCD$  be a quadrilateral satisfying  $\angle BCD=\angle CDA$ . Suppose rays  $AD$  and  $BC$  meet at  $E$ , and let  $\Gamma$  be the circumcircle of  $ABE$ . Let  $\Gamma_1$  be a circle tangent to ray  $CD$  past  $D$  at  $W$ , segment  $AD$  at  $X$ , and internally tangent to  $\Gamma$ . Similarly, let  $\Gamma_2$  be a circle tangent to ray  $DC$  past  $C$  at  $Y$ , segment  $BC$  at  $Z$ , and internally tangent to  $\Gamma$ . Let  $P$  be the intersection of  $WX$  and  $YZ$ , and suppose  $P$  lies on  $\Gamma$ . If  $F$  is the  $E$ -excenter of triangle  $ABE$ , and  $AB=544$ ,  $AE=2197$ ,  $BE=2299$ , then find  $m+n$ , where  $FP=\tfrac{m}{n}$  with  $m,n$  relatively prime positive integers.

*Proposed by Michael Kural*
solution_md:
We claim that  $FP$  is the  $F$ -median of the excentral triangle of  $ABE$ . If we prove this, all we have to do is divide the power of  $F$  with respect to  $(ABE)$  by the length of the  $F$ -median of the excentral triangle of  $ABE$ , and we can find the power of  $F$  by computing  $FE\cdot FM$ , where  $M$  is the midpoint of arc  $AB$ . So proving that  $FP$  is the  $F$ -median of the excentral triangle of  $ABE$  pretty much solves the problem.

Take  $ABE$  as the reference triangle. We’re trying to figure out where to put  $C$  on  $BE$  so that  $WX$  and  $YZ$  concur on  $(ABE)$ . Say  $CD$  intersects  $(ABE)$  at  $R$  and  $S$ . First we need the Sawayama Thebault Lemma from [here]("http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h18743p3558742"). It tells us that  $WX$  passes through the incenter of  $ARS$  and  $YZ$  passes through the incenter of  $BRS$ . Call these incenters  $I_a$  and  $I_b$ . If  $T$  is the midpoint of arc  $RS$ , then  $I_a$  lies on  $TA$  and  $I_b$  lies on  $TB$ . By the midpoint of arc lemma,  $TI_a=TI_b=TR=TS$ .  $I_a$  lies on  $WX$  and  $I_b$  lies on  $YZ$ , and we also know the angles that  $WX$  and  $YZ$  make relative to the sides of  $ABE$ . Thus we know the angles that  $I_aP$  and  $I_bP$  make relative to the sides of  $ABE$ . To get all of the relevant angles, we need to determine the angles that  $TA$  and  $TB$  make relative to the sides of  $ABE$ . We can find these angles by noting that  $OT$  is parallel to the  $E$ -angle bisector, where  $O$  is the circumcenter of  $ABE$ . After some straightforward but annoying angle chasing we get every angle in quadrilateral  $TI_aPI_b$ , including the angles made by the diagonal  $I_aI_b$  using  $TI_a=TI_b$  (but not the diagonal  $TP$ ). It turns out that if  $M$  is the midpoint of arc  $AEB$ , then  $TI_aPI_b$  is similar to  $MAFB$ . This means that  $\tfrac{\sin\angle I_aTP}{\sin\angle PTI_b}=\tfrac{\sin\angle AMF}{\sin\angle FMB}$ , or  $MF$  passes through  $P$ . Since  $(ABE)$  is the nine point circle of the excentral triangle of  $ABE$ ,  $M$  is the midpoint of the  $F$ -side of the excentral triangle of  $ABE$ . Thus  $FP$  is the  $F$ -median of the excentral triangle of  $ABE$ .

Eventually, we get  $FP=\tfrac{2431}{9}$ , making the final answer  $2431+9=\boxed{2440}$ .

stem_md:
Find the number of ordered pairs  $(P(x),Q(x))$  of polynomials with integer coefficients such that
\[
P(x)^2+Q(x)^2=\left(x^{4096}-1\right)^2.
\]

*Proposed by Michael Kural*
solution_md:
Copied from Google Docs:

Work over the Gaussian integers and factor as  $(P+Qi)(P-Qi)=(x^{4096}-1)^2$ . Note that  $x^{4096}-1$  factors over the Gaussian integers as  $(x-1)(x-i)(x^2-i)(x^4-i)(x^8-i)...(x^{1024}-i)$  times  $(x+1)(x+i)(x^2+i)(x^4+i)(x^8+i)...(x^{1024}+i)$ . Also,  $P+Qi$  and  $P-Qi$  are conjugates, so if  $r$  divides  $P+Qi$ , then the conjugate of  $r$  divides  $P-Qi$ . We need to pick some subset of the factors of  $(x^{4096}-1)^2$  to be the factors of  $P+Qi$  and choose the remaining factors of  $(x^{4096}-1)^2$  to be the factors of  $P-Qi$ . Start by distributing  $(x-1)^2$  to  $P+Qi$  and  $P-Qi$ . If  $x-1$  divides  $P+Qi$ , then  $x-1$  divides  $P-Qi$ , and vice versa. So the only possibility is to give  $x-1$  to  $P+Qi$  and the other  $x-1$  to  $P-Qi$ . The same argument holds for  $x+1$ . Now, if  $x-i$  divides  $P+Qi$ , then  $x+i$  divides  $P-Qi$ . So, there are three ways to give out  $(x-i)^2(x+i)^2$  to  $P+Qi$  and  $P-Qi$ : both get  $(x-i)(x+i)$ ,  $P+Qi$  gets  $(x-i)^2$  and  $P-Qi$  gets  $(x+i)^2$ , or  $P+Qi$  gets  $(x+i)^2$  and  $P-Qi$  gets  $(x-i)^2$ . The same logic holds for  $x^2+i$ ,  $x^4+i$ ,  $x^8+i$ , and so on until  $x^{1024}+i$ . That’s  $11$  different choices, for a total of  $3^{11}$  ways to choose which factors go where. Once we choose where the factors go, we can still multiply each of the factors by a unit. (For instance, if one of the factors is  $5-3i$  and the other factor is  $5+3i$ , that’ll give us  $P=5$  and  $Q=3$ . However, if we multiply by  $-1$ , we get  $P=-5$  and  $Q=-3$ . Multiplying by  $i$  gives  $P=3$ ,  $Q=5$  while multiplying by  $-i$  gives  $P=-3$ ,  $Q=-5$ . Also, if you want solutions like  $P=5, Q=-3$ , you have to alter the actual factor distribution (i.e. you can’t just multiply by a unit; you have to choose one of the other  $3^{11}$  factor distributions). Thus, multiplying by the number of units doesn’t miss any solutions.) There are four units ( $1$ ,  $-1$ ,  $i$ ,  $-i$ ), each of which gives  $3^{11}$  ways. Thus, the answer is  $4\cdot 3^{11}=\boxed{708588}$ .

<details><summary>Bad Gaussian</summary>Hmm the problem looks a lot like Pythagorean triples. Hmmmmmmm........... Wait a second. Didn't Euclid prove something about Pythagorean triples:  $$ a^2+b^2=c^2\implies a=k(x^2-y^2), b=2kxy, c=k(x^2+y^2) $$  Wait but the polynomial field sort of acts like the natural numbers right? So obviously:  $$ F(x)^2+G(x)^2=H(x)^2\implies F(x)=k(x)(f(x)^2-g(x)^2),G(x)=2k(x)f(x)g(x),H(x)=k(x)(f(x)^2+g(x)^2) $$  Okay so we have  $(x^{4096}-1)=k(x)(f(x)^2+g(x)^2)$ . Okay plug in  $x=\pm 1$ . Then we get  $0=k(\pm 1)(f(\pm 1)^2+g(\pm 1)^2)$ . Then either  $(x\pm 1)$  divides  $k(x)$  or  $f(x)^2+g(x)^2$ . It cannot divide  $f(x)^2+g(x)^2$  because then  $f(\pm 1)=g(\pm 1)=0$  implying that  $(x\pm 1)^2$  divides the LHS which it does not. So  $(x^2-1)$  divides  $k(x)$ . Say that we only select  $1$  term. Then we realize a property of the natural numbers which says that if a number is prime then it has  $0$  or  $1$  solutions (where order does not matter) for  $a^2+b^2=p$ . In polynomial language, this roughly correlates with if a polynomial is irreducible then it can be expressed in  $0$  or  $1$  non-negative solutions of  $f(x)^2+g(x)^2=h(x)$ . So there are  $2$  solutions with positive leading terms in our case. We claim that we can find  $2^{i-1}$  solutions given  $i$  factors. This follows from straightforward induction+binary argument that uses the fact that if  $f_1(x)^2+g_1(x)^2=h_1(x)$  and  $f_2(x)^2+g_2(x)^2=h_2(x)$  then   $$ (f_1(x)f_2(x)+g_1(x)g_2(x))^2+(f_1(x)g_2(x)-f_2(x)g_1(x))^2=h_1(x)h_2(x) $$    $$ (f_1(x)f_2(x)-g_1(x)g_2(x))^2+(f_1(x)g_2(x)+f_2(x)g_1(x))^2=h_1(x)h_2(x) $$  Thus the number of solutions is  $\binom{11}{0}+\binom{11}{1}*1+\binom{11}{2}*2...+\binom{11}{3}*4...+\binom{11}{11}*2^{10}$ . But notice that there  $8$  permutations of  $(a,b)$  namely  $(b,a)$ ,  $(-a,b)$ ,  $(a,-b)$ , $(-a,-b)$ ,  $(-b,a)$ ,  $(b,-a)$ , and  $(-b,-a)$  (only  $4$  for  $f(x)^2+g(x)^2=1$ ). So our grand total is   $$ \binom{11}{0}*4+\binom{11}{1}*8+\binom{11}{2}*16...+\binom{11}{3}*32...+\binom{11}{11}*2^{13} $$  which is just the binomial expansion of  $4(1+2)^{11}$</details>
^Official Solution of the Buttery Snorlax Team

Solved with Alex Zhao, David Dong, (Derek Liu), Elliott Liu, Jeffrey Chen, Luke Robitaille, Max Lu, Raymond Feng, and Ryan Yang. We work over \(\mathbb Z*[x]\). First: **Claim:** For all \(k\), the polynomials \(x^{2^k}+i\) and \(x^{2^k}-i\) are irreducible. [i]Proof.* The former follows from Eisenstein using \(p=1+i\) on \[(y+1)^{2^k}+i=y^{2^k}+{\underbrace{\cdots}_{\text{even}}}+(1+i),\] and analogously \(p=1-i\) on the latter. \(\blacksquare\) The complete factorization of the right-hand side is thus \begin{align*} (P+iQ)(P-iQ)&=\big[(x-1)(x+1)\cdot(x-i)(x+i)\cdot(x^2-i)(x^2+i) &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\cdots(x^{512}-i)(x^{512}+i)\cdot(x^{1024}-i)(x^{1024}+i)\big]^2. \end{align*} Now note that if \(T\in\mathbb Z[i][x]\) divides \(P+iQ\), then \(\overline T\) divides \(P-iQ\). Thus each of \(P+iQ\) and \(P-iQ\) must receive a factor of \((x-1)(x+1)\). Moreover for each \(k\), there are three ways to distribute the \((x^{2^k}+i)^2(x^{2^k}-i)^2\) factors: - \(P+iQ\) and \(P-iQ\) each receive a \((x^{2^k}+i)(x^{2^k}-i)\); - \(P+iQ\) receives a \((x^{2^k}+i)^2\) and \(P-iQ\) receives a \((x^{2^k}-i)^2\); or - \(P+iQ\) receives a \((x^{2^k}-i)^2\) and \(P-iQ\) receives a \((x^{2^k}+i)^2\). Evidently each of the aforementioned distribution of factors works. Finally there are four ways to choose the leading coefficients, so the answer is \(4\cdot3^{11}\).

stem_md:
Let  $ABC$  be an acute scalene triangle with incenter  $I$ , and let  $M$  be the circumcenter of triangle  $BIC$ .  Points  $D$ ,  $B'$ , and  $C'$  lie on side  $BC$  so that  $ \angle BIB' = \angle CIC' = \angle IDB = \angle IDC = 90^{\circ} $ .  Define  $P = \overline{AB} \cap \overline{MC'}$ ,  $Q = \overline{AC} \cap \overline{MB'}$ ,  $S = \overline{MD} \cap \overline{PQ}$ , and  $K = \overline{SI} \cap \overline{DF}$ , where segment  $EF$  is a diameter of the incircle selected so that  $S$  lies in the interior of segment  $AE$ .  It is known that  $KI=15x$ ,  $SI=20x+15$ ,  $BC=20x^{5/2}$ , and  $DI=20x^{3/2}$ , where  $x = \tfrac ab(n+\sqrt p)$  for some positive integers  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $n$ ,  $p$ , with  $p$  prime and  $\gcd(a,b)=1$ . Compute  $a+b+n+p$ .

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md:
Say  $MP$  and  $MQ$  meet  $(ABC)$  again at  $P’$  and  $Q’$ . Let  $T$  and  $U$  be the feet of the altitudes from  $I$  to  $CA$  and  $AB$ , and say  $BI$  and  $CI$  meet  $(ABC)$  again at  $T’$  and  $U’$ . Triangles  $DTU$  and  $MT’U’$  are homothetic, so  $DM$ ,  $TT’$ , and  $UU’$  concur at their center of homothety. Redefine  $S$  as this center of homothety. We claim that  $S$  is the same as the old  $S$ . That’s equivalent to showing that  $S$  lies on  $PQ$ . If we show that  $S$  lies on  $BQ’$  and  $CP’$ , then we’ll be done by Pascal on  $ABQ’MP’C$ . So let’s show that  $S$  lies on  $BQ’$  and  $CP’$ . Since  $S$  is the center of homothety between  $DTU$  and  $MT’U’$ , it’s also the center of homothety between  $(DTU)$  and  $(MT’U’)$ , i.e.  $(I)$  and  $(O)$ . In fact, it’s the exsimilicenter of  $(I)$  and  $(O)$ . So by Monge d’Alembert and inversion,  $S$  is the isogonal conjugate of the Nagel point. We want to show that  $S$  lies on  $CP’$ . That’s equivalent to showing that  $\tfrac{\sin\angle BMC’}{\sin\angle C’MI}=\tfrac{\sin\angle BCS}{\sin\angle SCA}$ . Say the  $C$ -excircle of  $ABC$  hits  $AB$  at  $X$ ,  $AC$  at  $A’$ , and  $BC$  at  $B’$ . Angle chasing yields  $CA’B’X$  is similar to  $MBIC’$ , so  $\tfrac{\sin\angle BMC’}{\sin\angle C’MI}=\tfrac{\sin\angle A’CX}{\sin\angle XCB’}$ . Since  $S$  is the isogonal conjugate of the Nagel point,  $CS$  and  $CX$  are isogonal, i.e.  $\tfrac{\sin\angle A’CX}{\sin\angle XCB’}=\tfrac{\sin\angle BCS}{\sin\angle SCA}$ . Stringing these equalities together gives  $\tfrac{\sin\angle BMC’}{\sin\angle C’MI}=\tfrac{\sin\angle BCS}{\sin\angle SCA}$ . Thus  $S$  lies on  $CP’$ . By the same reasoning,  $S$  lies on  $BQ’$ . So by Pascal on  $ABQ’MP’C$ ,  $S$  lies on  $PQ$ , i.e.  $S$  is the same as the old  $S$ .

Now we need to deal with  $K$ . Let  $D’$  be the point diametrically opposite  $D$  in  $(I)$  and say  $D’E$  intersects  $OI$  at  $K’$ . Since  $K’I=KI$ , we’ll know everything about  $K$  if we know everything about  $K’$ . So let’s find out stuff about  $K’$ . We claim that the homothety at  $S$  sending  $(I)$  to  $(O)$  also sends  $K’$  to  $I$ . If  $Y$  is the midpoint of arc  $BAC$  and  $Z$  is the tangency point between the  $A$ -mixtilinear incircle and  $(O)$ , then this homothety sends  $E$  to  $Z$  and  $D’$  to  $Y$ . So we want to show that  $I$  lies on  $YZ$ , or equivalently that  $ZI$  bisects  $\angle BZC$ . Since  $\angle BZC = 180-\angle A$ , that’s the same as showing that  $\angle BZI=90-\tfrac{A}{2}$ . Let  $V$  be the tangency point between that  $A$ -mixtilinear incircle and  $AB$ , and say  $ZV$  intersects  $(O)$  at  $V’$ . The homothety centered at  $Z$  sending the  $A$ -mixtilinear incircle to  $(O)$  also sends  $V$  to  $V’$ . Thus the tangent at  $V’$  to  $(O)$  is parallel to  $AB$ , i.e.  $V’$  is the midpoint of arc  $AB$ . Thus  $\angle BZV=\tfrac{C}{2}$ . Angle-chasing yields  $\angle BIV=\tfrac{C}{2}$ , so  $BVIZ$  is cyclic. Thus  $\angle BZI=\angle AVI=90-\tfrac{A}{2}$ , i.e.  $ZI$  bisects  $\angle BZC$ . So  $I$  lies on  $YZ$ , implying that the homothety at  $S$  sending  $(I)$  to  $(O)$  also sends  $K’$  to  $I$ . Some length chasing yields  $\tfrac{KI}{IO}=\tfrac{r}{R}$ , where  $r$  is the inradius of  $ABC$  and  $R$  is the circumradius of  $ABC$ .

Remember also that  $\tfrac{SI}{SO}=\tfrac{r}{R}$  and  $IO=\sqrt{R^2-2Rr}$ . Length chasing yields  $KI=\tfrac{r}{R}\sqrt{R^2-2Rr}$  and  $SI=\tfrac{r}{R-r}\sqrt{R^2-2Rr}$ . Dividing these two equations (remembering that  $KI=15x$  and  $SI=20x+15$ ) gives  $\tfrac{r}{R}=\tfrac{x+3}{4x+3}$ . If we plug this into  $KI=\tfrac{r}{R}\sqrt{R^2-2Rr}$  (remembering that  $KI=15x$  and  $r=20x^{\tfrac{3}{2}}$ ), we end up with  $9=16x-32x\tfrac{r}{R}=16x-\tfrac{32x(x+3)}{4x+3}$ , a quadratic in  $x$  with solutions  $x=\pm\tfrac{3}{16}(7+\sqrt{73})$ .  $x$  is positive, so  $x=\tfrac{3}{16}(7+\sqrt{73})$ , making the answer  $3+16+7+73=\boxed{99}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $S$  be the value of
\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{d(n) + \sum_{m=1}^{\nu_2(n)}(m-3)d\left(\frac{n}{2^m}\right)}{n},\]
where  $d(n)$  is the number of divisors of  $n$  and  $\nu_2(n)$  is the exponent of  $2$  in the prime factorization of  $n$ . If  $S$  can be expressed as  $(\ln m)^n$  for positive integers  $m$  and  $n$ , find  $1000n + m$ .

*Proposed by Robin Park*
solution_md:
While testsolving OMO, here's an "elementary" solution I found. It's not 100% rigorous, but hopefully people above asking about whether their approach worked will find this helpful. (copy-pasted from an email among OMO writers)


I'll find \[ \lim_{\ell \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{n = 1}^{2^\ell} \frac{d(n)+\sum_{m = 1}^{v_2(n)} (m-3) d(\frac{n}{2^m}) }{n} \]

Now we compute in the above sum the coefficient of  $d(x).$  Firstly, ignore the extra  $d(x)/x$  terms. Let  $j_x = \lfloor log_2 2^\ell / x \rfloor$ . Then the coefficient of  $d(x)$  is clearly \[ \sum_{i = 1}^{j_x} \frac{i-3}{x \cdot 2^i} = \frac{1}{x} \cdot 
\left(-1-\frac{j_x-1}{2^{j_x}} \right) \]

Adding back in the  $d(x)/x$ , the coefficient is  $\frac{1-j_x}{2^{j_x}}$ . So we just need to compute \[ \sum_{n = 1}^{2^\ell} \frac{1-j_x}{2^{j_x}} \frac{d(x)}{x} = \sum_{k = 0}^\ell \frac{1-(\ell-k)}{2^{\ell-k}} \cdot \sum_{n = 2^{k-1}+1}^{2^k} \frac{d(n)}{n} .\]

I just grouped the terms that had the same  $j_x$  together. Now for good heuristics! We're going to approximate  $\sum_{i = 1}^n \frac{d(i)}{i}.$  Look at the contribution that the number  $k$  gives. It is equal to  $\frac{1}{k} + \frac{1}{2k} + \ldots + \frac{1}{k \cdot \lfloor n/k \rfloor} \approx \frac{\ln(n/k)}{k} = \frac{\ln n - \ln k}{k}$ .

Summing: \[ \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\ln n - \ln k}{k} \approx (\ln n)^2 - \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{\ln k}{k} \]

Now we're in position to approximate the thing above: \[ \sum_{n = 2^{k-1}+1}^{2^k} \frac{d(n)}{n} = \sum_{1}^{2^k} \frac{d(n)}{n} - \sum_{1}^{2^{k-1}} \frac{d(n)}{n} \] \[ \approx (\ln 2^k)^2 - \sum_{n = 1}^{2^k} \frac{\ln n}{n} - (\ln 2^{k-1})^2 + \sum_{n = 1}^{2^{k-1}} \frac{\ln n}{n} \] \[ = (2k-1) (\ln 2)^2 - \sum_{n  = 2^{k-1}+1}^{2^k} \frac{\ln n}{n} \] \[ \approx (2k-1) (\ln 2)^2 - (k-1) (\ln 2)^2 = k (\ln 2)^2.\]

The last thing follows by assuming that every numerator is approximately  $(k-1) (\ln 2)$  (since they are all ~ $2^{k-1}$ ) Then the denominators are  $\frac{1}{2^{k-1}+1} + \frac{1}{2^{k-1}+2} + \dots + \frac{1}{2^k} \approx \ln(2^k) - \ln(2^{k-1}) = \ln 2.$  Now our finish is easy. Substitue this into the above forumla: \[ \lim_{\ell \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{k = 0}^\ell \frac{1-(\ell-k)}{2^{\ell-k}} \cdot \sum_{n = 2^{k-1}+1}^{2^k} \frac{d(n)}{n} \] \[ \approx \lim_{\ell \rightarrow \infty} (\ln 2)^2 \cdot \sum_{k = 0}^{\ell} \frac{1-(\ell-k)}{2^{\ell-k}} \cdot k = 4 (\ln 2)^2 \] after some easy computations.

The sum isn’t absolutely convergent, but this sum is:

\[\lim_{t\to1^+}\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{d(n)+\sum_{m=1}^{v_2(n)}(m-3)d(\frac{n}{2^m})}{n^t}\]

Now we can start moving terms around… use  $d(\frac{n}{2^m}) = d(n)\frac{v_2(n) - m + 1}{v_2(n) + 1}$  to simplify the sum to

\[\frac16\lim_{t\to1^+}\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left[\frac{d(n)}{n^t}(v_2(n)^2-7v_2(n)+6)\right]\]

Then use

\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{d(n)}{n^t}=\sum_{a=1}^\infty\sum_{b=1}^\infty\frac1{(ab)^t}=\left[\sum_{a=1}^\infty\frac1{a^t}\right]^2=[\zeta(t)]^2\]

\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{d(n)v_2(n)}{n^t}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{kd(2^k(2n-1))}{(2^k(2n-1))^t}=\left(\frac{k(k+1)}{2^{kt}}\right)\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{d(2n-1)}{(2n-1)^t}\right)\]
\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{d(n)v_2(n)^2}{n^t}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{k^2d(2^k(2n-1))}{(2^k(2n-1))^t}=\left(\frac{k^2(k+1)}{2^{kt}}\right)\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{d(2n-1)}{(2n-1)^t}\right)\]

which leaves us with the task of evaluating

\[\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{k(k+1)}{2^{kt}}=\frac{2^{2t+1}}{(2^t-1)^3}\]
\[\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{k^2(k+1)}{2^{kt}}=\frac{2^{2t+1}(2^t+2)}{(2^t-1)^4}\]
\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{d(2n-1)}{(2n-1)^t}=\sum_{a=1}^\infty\sum_{b=1}^\infty\frac{1}{(2a-1)^t(2b-1)^t}=\left[\sum_{a=1}^\infty\frac{1}{(2a-1)^t}\right]^2=\left[\left(1-\frac1{2^t}\right)\zeta(t)\right]^2\]

Finally it's just

\[\left[\lim_{t\to1^+}\frac{2^t-2}{2^t-1}\zeta(t)\right]^2=\ln^24\]

*Proposed by Evan Chen*

stem_md:
Farmer John has a (flexible) fence of length  $L$  and two straight walls that intersect at a corner perpendicular to each other. He knows that if he doesn't use any walls, he call enclose an maximum possible area of  $A_0$ , and when he uses one of the walls or both walls, he gets a maximum of area of  $A_1$  and  $A_2$  respectively. If  $n=\frac{A_1}{A_0}+\frac{A_2}{A_1}$ , find  $\lfloor 1000n\rfloor$ .

*Proposed by Yannick Yao*
solution_md:
<details><summary>because I like rigor</summary>We first compute  $A_0$ . By the isoperimetric inequality,  $\frac{L^2}{A}\geq4\pi$ , or  $A\leq\frac{L^2}{4\pi}$ , equality holding when the shape is a circle. Thus,  $A_0=\frac{L^2}{4\pi}$ .

Now, to compute  $A_1$ . Assume a shape gives maximal area. Reflect it over the wall used to get a new shape of perimeter  $2L$ . Again by the isoperimetric inequality,  $\frac{\left(2L\right)^2}{A}\geq4\pi$ , or  $A\leq\frac{L^2}{\pi}$ , equality holding when the shape is a circle, or the original shape is a semicircle. Thus,  $A_1=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{L^2}{\pi}=\frac{L^2}{2\pi}$ .

Now, to compute  $A_2$ . Again assume a shape gives maximal area. Reflect it over one wall used to get a new shape, and reflect this shape over the other wall to get another shape with perimeter  $4L$ . By the isoperimetric inequality,  $\frac{\left(4L\right)^2}{A}\geq4\pi$ , or  $A\leq\frac{4L^2}{\pi}$ , equality holding when the shape is a circle, or the original shape is a quartercircle. Thus,  $A_2=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{4L^2}{\pi}=\frac{L^2}{\pi}$ .

Thus,  $n=\frac{A_1}{A_0}+\frac{A_2}{A_1}=2+2=4$ , so  $\lfloor1000n\rfloor=\boxed{4000}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/Online Math Open Problems/2015 Online Math Open Problems/1164275.json

stem_md:
The two numbers  $0$  and  $1$  are initially written in a row on a chalkboard. Every minute thereafter, Denys writes the number  $a+b$  between all pairs of consecutive numbers  $a$ ,  $b$  on the board. How many odd numbers will be on the board after  $10$  such operations?

*Proposed by Michael Kural*
solution_md:
First, reduce all numbers to  $\pmod {2}$ . This is okay.
Let  $a_n$  be the number of  $00$ ,  $b_n$  be the number of  $01$ ,  $c_n$  be the number of  $10$ ,  $d_n$  be the number of  $11$ , in adjacent numbers after  $n$  operations.

Lemma 1.  $a_n+b_n+c_n+d_n=2^n$ .
Proof. Clearly the number of numbers on the board satisfy a recurrence  $A_n=2A_{n-1}-1$ , so  $A_n=2^n+1$  since  $A_1=3$ .
Therefore, we have the sum of all adjacent sets,  $a_n+b_n+c_n+d_n$ , equal to  $A_n-1$ , which is  $2^n$  as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Lemma 2.  $a_n=0$ ,  $b_{n+1}=b_n+d_n$ ,  $c_{n+1}=c_n+d_n$ ,  $d_{n+1}=b_n+c_n$ .
Proof. Operations map  $00 \mapsto 000$ ,  $01 \mapsto 011$ ,  $10 \mapsto 110$ ,  $11 \mapsto 101$ . Now check for the patterns after the mapping. Note that there are no overcounts at all. Now we have  $a_{n+1}=2a_n$ , so since  $a_1=0$ , we have  $a_n=0$ . The rest follows easily.  $\blacksquare$ Lemma 3. Let the number of  $1$ s after  $n$  operations be  $X_n$ .
We have  $X_n=X_{n-1}+b_{n-1}+c_{n-1}$ .
Proof. The maps  $01 \mapsto 011$  and  $10 \mapsto 110$  gives one more  $1$  each. The proof is done.  $\blacksquare$ Lemma 4. Let  $k_n=b_n+c_n$ . We have  $k_n=\frac{2}{3} \cdot 2^n+ \frac{1}{3} \cdot (-1)^n$ .
Proof. We have  $k_n=b_n+c_n=b_{n-1}+c_{n-1}+2d_{n-1}=b_{n-1}+c_{n-1}+2(b_{n-2}+c_{n-2})=k_{n-1}+2k_{n-2}$ .
The characteristic equation for this recurrence is  $x^2-x-2=0$ .
Solving with  $k_1=1, k_2=3$ , we have  $k_n=\frac{2}{3} \cdot 2^n+ \frac{1}{3} \cdot (-1)^n$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Now we have  $X_1=2$  and  $X_n=X_{n-1}+\frac{2}{3} \cdot 2^{n-1}+\frac{1}{3} \cdot (-1)^{n-1}$ .
Solving for  $X_{10}$ , we have  $X_{10}=2+\frac{2}{3} \cdot (2+2^2+ \cdots 2^9) + \frac{1}{3} \cdot (-1+1- \cdots -1) = 2+\frac{2}{3} \cdot (1022) -\frac{1}{3} = 2+\frac{2043}{3}=2+681= \boxed{683}$  as the desired answer.

stem_md: For any positive integer  $n$ , define a function  $f$  by \[f(n)=2n+1-2^{\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor+1}.\] Let  $f^m$  denote the function  $f$  applied  $m$  times.. solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>If we work in binary, note that the function will eventually end in a sequence of  $k$  1's, where  $k$  is the original number of 1's in the number. Let  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  be the distinct roots of the polynomial  $P(x) = x^3 - 10x^2 + x - 2015$ .
The cubic polynomial  $Q(x)$  is monic and has distinct roots  $bc-a^2$ ,  $ca-b^2$ ,  $ab-c^2$ .
What is the sum of the coefficients of  $Q$ ?

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md:
<details><summary>storage, elegant problem!</summary>\[Q(1)=(1-bc+a^2)(1-ca+b^2)(1-ab+c^2)\]
and note  $ab+bc+ca=1$  so looking at the factor  $1-bc+a^2$  we have
\[1-bc+a^2=a(a+b+c).\]
Multiplying them together, \[Q(1)=abc(a+b+c)^3=\boxed{2015000}.\]
\[\mathbb{Q.E.D.}\]</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/Online Math Open Problems/2015 Online Math Open Problems/1164281.json

candidates: <details><summary>Solution</summary>From the given information, we can express  $Q$  as  $Q(x)=(x+a^2-bc)(x+b^2-ca)(x+c^2-ab)$ . The sum of the coefficients is found plugging in  $x=1$ . Thus, the desired sum is  $(1+a^2-bc)(1+b^2-ca)(1+c^2-ab)$ . By Vieta's on  $P(x)$ , we find  $ab+bc+ca=1$ . Thus,  $ab=1-bc-ca$ ,  $bc=1-ab-ca$ , and  $ca=1-ab-bc$ . Plugging this into the expression for the sum of the roots of  $Q$ , we get  $(a^2+ab+ac)(b^2+ab+bc)(c^2+ac+bc)=abc(a+b+c)^3$ . From Vieta's again, we have  $a+b+c=10$  and  $abc=2015$ . Thus, our answer is  $2015\cdot10^3=\boxed{2015000}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>The sum of the coefficients of  $Q$  is \[Q(1) = \prod_{\text{cyc}} \left(1 - bc+a^2\right) = \frac{1}{abc}\prod_{\text{cyc}} \left(a - abc+a^3\right)\] \[ = \frac{1}{abc}\prod_{\text{cyc}} \left(\left(a+a^3\right) - abc\right) = \frac{1}{abc}\prod_{\text{cyc}} \left(\left(10a^2+2015\right) - 2015\right) \] \[= \frac{1}{abc}\cdot 1000 (abc)^2 = 1000abc = 2015000.\]</details>

Assume the roots of the polynomial  $P(x)=x^3-10x^2+x-2015$  are  $\alpha,\beta,\gamma.$  We have to find a monic cubic polynomial with distinct roots  $\alpha\beta-\gamma^2, \beta\gamma-\alpha^2, \gamma\alpha-\beta^2.$  By Vieta's Relation we get,   $$ \alpha+\beta+\gamma=10 $$     $$ \alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=1 $$     $$ \alpha\beta\gamma=2015 $$   Therefore the sum of roots of  $Q(x)$  is   $$ S_1=\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha\beta-\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha^2=1-98\implies\boxed{S_1=-97} $$   Sum of roots taken two at a time we get,   $$ S_2=\alpha\beta\gamma(\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha)+(\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha^2\beta^2)-(\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha^3\beta+\sum_{cyc}{}\beta^3\alpha)\implies 20150-40299-(\sum_{cyc}{}\alpha^3(\beta+\gamma)+\sum_{cyc}{}\beta^3(\alpha+\gamma) $$     $$ -20149-(\alpha^3\beta+\beta^3\gamma+\gamma^3\alpha+\alpha\beta^3+\beta\gamma^3+\gamma\alpha^3=\alpha^3(\beta+\gamma)+\beta^3(\alpha+\gamma)+\gamma^3(\alpha+\beta))\implies\alpha^3(10-\alpha)+\beta^3(10-\beta)+\gamma^3(10-\gamma) $$     $$ 10\alpha^3-\alpha^4+10\beta^3-\beta^4+10\gamma^3-\gamma^4=10(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3)-\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4\implies121816450-121836502\implies20052-20149 $$     $$ \boxed{S_2=-97} $$  And finally we have to find the product of roots   $$ S_3=(\alpha\beta-\gamma^2)(\gamma\beta-\alpha^2)(\gamma\alpha-\beta^2)=\sum_{cyc}{}(\alpha^3\beta^3)-\sum_{cyc}{}(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3)\alpha\beta\gamma\implies\boxed{S_3=-2014999} $$  Therefore we get the cubic as   $$ \boxed{Q(x)=x^3+97x^2-97x+2014999} $$   Therefore the sum of digits of  $Q(x)$  is  $\boxed{2015000.}$  
Vieta's Relation!!!! :love:

stem_md:
You live in an economy where all coins are of value  $1/k$  for some positive integer  $k$  (i.e.  $1, 1/2, 1/3, \dots$ ). You just recently bought a coin exchanging machine, called the *Cape Town Machine*. For any integer  $n > 1$ , this machine can take in  $n$  of your coins of the same value, and return a coin of value equal to the sum of values of those coins (provided the coin returned is part of the economy). Given that the product of coins values that you have is  $2015^{-1000}$ , what is the maximum numbers of times you can use the machine over all possible starting sets of coins?

*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Hint</summary>If all our conversions are  $a$   $\frac{1}{a}$  pieces to  $1$  pieces, then it is clear that the answer is  $[1000/5] + [1000/13] + [1000/31] = 308$  ( $[x]$  is floor notation).</details>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let us choose the starting coins to maximize the coin product value (as long as it is greater than or equal to  $2015^{-1000}$ ) and the number of times we can use the machine.

Suppose we have a conversion of  $a$  pieces of  $\frac{1}{ab}$  coin to one  $\frac{1}{b}$  coin on the first move ( $a, b$  not necessarily distinct). Consider a conversion of  $a$  pieces of  $\frac{1}{a}$  coin to one  $1$  coin, and a lone  $\frac{1}{b}$  coin. This second conversion is equally if not more economical (no pun intended) as it is the first conversion with a bonus  $1$  coin thrown in. However, the product of the  $a$   $\frac{1}{a}$  coins and the  $\frac{1}{b}$  coins' value is greater than that of the  $a$   $\frac{1}{ab}$  coins, contradicting the maximality of our configuration. Thus the conversion on the first move must be  $a$   $\frac{1}{a}$  coins to a  $1$  coin. Now repeat the above argument on the other coins (clearly the  $1$  coin cannot be used in a subsequent exchange) to prove that each move turns  $a$   $\frac{1}{a}$  coins to a  $1$  coin, so answer is in hint.</details>

stem_md:
Let  $a_1$ ,  $a_2, \dots, a_{2015}$  be a sequence of positive integers in  $[1,100]$ .
Call a nonempty contiguous subsequence of this sequence *good* if the product of the integers in it leaves a remainder of  $1$  when divided by  $101$ .
In other words, it is a pair of integers  $(x, y)$  such that  $1 \le x \le y \le 2015$  and \[a_xa_{x+1}\dots a_{y-1}a_y \equiv 1 \pmod{101}. \]Find the minimum possible number of good subsequences across all possible  $(a_i)$ .

*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $b_0=1$  and   $$ b_n=\prod_{m=1}^{n}a_n \pmod{101}. $$   Then we can see that a good subsequence occurs whenever  $b_n=b_m$  for  $0\le n<m\le 2015$ . Since 101 is prime, it is possible to choose a sequence  $a_n$  such that we obtain whatever sequence  $b_n$  we desire. In order to minimize the number of good subsequences, we should make the values in  $b_n$  as evenly distributed as possible. Since there are 2016  $b_n$  which can have any of 100 possible values, there will be 84   $m$   for which   $b_{n}=m$   20 times, and 16   $m$   for which   $b_{n}=m$   21 times. Thus the answer is   $$ 84\dbinom{20}{2}+16\dbinom{21}{2}=19320 $$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/Withdrawn USA Contests/Online Math Open Problems/2015 Online Math Open Problems/1164283.json

Copied over from Spreadsheets:

<details><summary>Solution?</summary>Let  $g$  be a primitive root of  $101$  (which must exist, since  $101$  is prime). Then by the properties of primitive roots, we can express each term  $a_i$  as  $g^{x_i}$  for some power  $x_i$ . So the problem reduces to finding the minimal number of sequences  $x_i,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_k$  for which \[ x_{i}+x_{i+1}+\ldots+x_{k} \equiv 0 \pmod{100}.\] Consider the first term of this sequence. When we add on a consecutive term, the total sum has to be distinct from any previous cumulative sums each time in order for there not to be any subsequence which sums to  $100$ . Then there are  $99$  distinct nonzero residues (we never want zero), so by the Pigeonhole Principle, when we get to  $100$  terms, we must have a subsequence that sums to  $0$  modulo  $100$ . After this term, we simply repeat the sequence (otherwise, we would find a smaller subsequence, which we don't want). A valid sequence is \[ 1, 1, 1, \ldots, 1. \] Then the desired sum is \[ 20\cdot2015 - (99+199+\ldots+1999)=19320. \]</details>
Would it be possible to use Wilson's theorem for this problem? I considered it for this problem since  $101$  is prime, and the integers ranged from  $1$  to  $100$ .

@above, I think Wilson's Theorem would be hard to use. Wilson's theorem is in fact a very weak statement about the integers  $1, 2, \dots, p-1.$  There are stronger results about the structure of the integers  $1, 2, \dots, p-1$ , such as they all have an inverse, or that they have a primitive root / generator. These would be more useful. For this problem, the existence of inverses (which allows division), is really the most important property.

stem_md:
A regular  $2015$ -simplex  $\mathcal P$  has  $2016$  vertices in  $2015$ -dimensional space such that the distances between every pair of vertices are equal. Let  $S$  be the set of points contained inside  $\mathcal P$  that are closer to its center than any of its vertices. The ratio of the volume of  $S$  to the volume of   $\mathcal P$  is  $\frac mn$ , where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers. Find the remainder when  $m+n$  is divided by  $1000$ .

*Proposed by James Lin*
solution_md: <details><summary>Sketch since I'm lazy</summary>Let the vertices be  $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{2016}$  with centroid  $G$ . Then the planes that perpendicularly bisect segments  $\overline{A_nG}$  for all  $n$  and the simplex bound the desired region. The bounded volume will be the volume of the original  $2015$ -simplex minus the volume of  $2016$  smaller similar  $2015$ -simplices whose "altitudes" are half the length  $\overline{A_nG}$ . Bash to get  $\boxed{321.}$</details>

stem_md:
Let  $x_1 \dots, x_{42}$ , be real numbers such that  $5x_{i+1}-x_i-3x_ix_{i+1}=1$  for each  $1 \le i \le 42$ , with  $x_1=x_{43}$ . Find all the product of all possible values for  $x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_{42}$ .

*Proposed by Michael Ma*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Why did I even</summary>We have  $x_{i+1}=\frac{x_i+1}{5-3x_i}$ . Let  $x_{n+1}=\frac{a_nx_1+b_n}{c_nx_1+d_n}$ .
We have  $a_1=1, b_1=1, c_1=-3, d_1=5$ .
The recursion gives  $a_{n+1}=a_n+c_n, b_{n+1}=b_n+d_n$ ,  $c_{n+1}=5c_n-3a_n, d_{n+1}=5d_n-3b_n$ .
Solving this gives  $a_n=-2^{2n-1}+3 \cdot 2^{n-1}$ ,  $b_n = 2^{2n-1}-2^{n-1}$ ,  $c_n=3 \cdot 2^{n-1} - 3 \cdot 2^{2n-1}$ ,  $d_n=3 \cdot 2^{2n-1} - 2^{n-1}$ .

From  $x_1=x_{43}$ , we have  $x_1 = \frac{a_{42}x_1+b_{42}}{c_{42}x_1+d_{42}}$ .
Now this is a quadratic. Note that  $x_1=1$  gives a solution.
Expanding this quadratic gives  $(3 \cdot 2^{41}- 3\cdot 2^{83})x^2_1 +(2^{85}-2^{43})x_1 + \text{blah} = 0$ .
Now vieta's gives that the sum of two solutions is  $\frac{2^{85}-2^{43}}{3(2^{83}-2^{41})} = \frac{4}{3}$ .
Therefore, the other possible value of  $x_1$  must be  $\frac{1}{3}$ .

If  $x_1=1$ , we have  $x_i=1$ , so the sum is  $42$ .

If  $x_1=\frac{1}{3}$ , we have  $x_i=\frac{1}{3}$ , so the sum is  $14$ .

The desired answer will be  $42 \cdot 14 = \boxed{588}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution 17</summary>Let  $a=x_1$  for simplicity.  Note that the recurrence simplifies to \[x_{i+1}(5-3x_i)=1+x_i\quad\implies\quad x_{i+1}=\dfrac{1+x_i}{5-3x_i}.\] This means that  $x_2=\tfrac{1+a}{5-3a}$ .  Now we prove a lemma.**LEMMA:** Every term  $x_k$  is of the form  $\tfrac{ma+n}{pa+q}$  for some reals  $m$ ,  $n$ ,  $p$ , and  $q$ .

*Proof.* Straightforward.  (Use induction plug in to the definition of the  $x_i$  shown above.)

Now, the equation  $x_1=x_{43}$  becomes  $a=\tfrac{ma+n}{pa+q}$ , which is a quadratic.  As a result, there can be at most two starting values of  $a$  for which  $x_1=x_{43}$ .

However, note that the equality  $x_1=x_2$  has two solutions as well, so *all* sequences which satisfy  $x_1=x_{43}$  must be constant.  As before, let  $a$  be the first term.  Plugging in  $x_1=x_2=a$  yields  $3a^2-4a+1=0$ .  From here we can either solve for  $a$  or use Vieta's to get that the product of all possible values of  $x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_{42}$  is  $42^2\cdot\tfrac13=\boxed{588}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Favorite</summary>We have  $(5-3x_i)x_{i+1} = 1 + x_i$  for each  $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 42$ . Note that if  $5-3x_i = 0$ , then the LHS is zero but the RHS is nonzero, a contradiction. Hence, we may divide by  $5-3x_i$  to get \[x_{i+1} = \dfrac{1+x_i}{5-3x_i}\] for  $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 42$ . If we define the function  $f(t) = \dfrac{1+t}{5-3t}$  for  $t \neq 5/3$ , then we have  $x_2 = f(x_1), x_3 = f(x_2), \ldots, x_{42} = f(x_{41}), x_1 = f(x_{42})$ . Then  $x_1, \ldots, x_{42}$  are fixed points of the function  $g = f^{42}$ . But if a function  $h(x) = \dfrac{a+bx}{c+dx}$ , then  $h(h(x))$  takes the same form: \[h(h(x)) = \dfrac{a + b \cdot \frac{a+bx}{c+dx}}{c + d \cdot \frac{a+bx}{c+dx}} = \dfrac{a(c+dx) + b(a+bx)}{c(c+dx) + d(a+bx)} = \dfrac{(b^2+ad)x + (ab+ac)}{(bd+cd)x + (ad+c^2)}.\] Hence,  $g$  is also a quotient of two linear functions, so the equation  $g(t) = t$  has at most two solutions. But if  $f(t) = t$ , then  $g(t) = t$  as well, so we can try to solve the equation  $f(t) = t$  (hopefully it has two solutions!) We have  $\dfrac{1+t}{5-3t} = t$ , whose solutions are  $t = 1, 1/3$ . So indeed, each  $x_i$  is  $1$  or  $1/3$ , and since these values are fixed points of  $f$ , the  $x_i$  must all be equal. Therefore, the solutions are all  $x_i = 1$  or all  $x_i = 1/3$ , so the answer is \[42 \cdot 42/3 = 588.\]</details>

<details><summary>Using eigenvectors</summary>If we let  $A= \left( \begin{matrix} 1&1 -3&5 \end{matrix} \right)$  and  $v = \left( \begin{matrix} x_1  1 \end{matrix} \right)$ , then interpreting  $v$  as the quotient of its top and bottom element, we find that the condition  $x_1 = x_{43}$  is equivalent to  $v$  being an eigenvector of  $A^{42}$ . But any eigenvector of  $A$  is also an eigenvector of  $A^{42}$ , and  $A^{42}$  has two distinct eigenvalues  $2^{42}$  and  $4^{42}$  and is not diagonal, so  $A^{42}$  has the same eigenvectors as  $A$ , which are easily seen to be  $\left( \begin{matrix} 1  1 \end{matrix} \right)$  and  $\left( \begin{matrix} 1  3 \end{matrix} \right)$ , or 1 and  $\frac13$ , so the answer is  $42\times 14 = 588$ .</details>

<details><summary>Might as well</summary>Rearrange the given equation to get \[x_{i+1}=\frac{1+x_i}{5-3x_i}.\] I claim that \[x_{k}=\frac{(2^{k-1}-1)-(2^{k-1}-3)x_1}{3(2^{k-1})-1-(3(2^{k-1})-3)x_1}\] for  $2\leq k\leq 42$ . We prove this using induction.

stem_md:
Given a (nondegenrate) triangle  $ABC$  with positive integer angles (in degrees), construct squares  $BCD_1D_2, ACE_1E_2$  outside the triangle. Given that  $D_1, D_2, E_1, E_2$  all lie on a circle, how many ordered triples  $(\angle A, \angle B, \angle C)$  are possible?

*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md:
<details><summary>complex bash :D</summary>We put the triangle on the complex plane, such that  $C=c=1$ ,  $B=b=\text{cis}y$ , and  $A=a=\text{cis}x$ . Notice that the perpendicular bisector of  $D_1D_2$  and  $E_1E_2$  both pass through  $0$ . Thus it suffices to find the triangles such that  $OE_1=OD_1$ . We have  $D_1=d=i(b-1)+1$ ,  $E_1=e=-i(a-1)+1$ . We want  $\dfrac{d+e}{d-e}=\dfrac{i(b-a)+2}{i(b+a-2)}$  imaginary, or  $\dfrac{i(b-a)+2}{b+a-2}$  real. Thus we want
\[\dfrac{i(b-a)+2}{b+a-2}=\dfrac{2-i(\overline{b}-\overline{a})}{\overline{b}+\overline{a}-2}.\]
Plugging in  $1/b$  for  $\overline{b}$  and similarly for  $a$ , then bashing tells us this is equivalent to
\[(ab-1)(a+b+(a-b)i)=0.\]
The case  $ab-1=0$  tells us all isosceles triangle work, giving us  $89$  possibilities. As for  $a+b+(a-b)i=0$ , we expand to get
\[\cos x-\sin x+\cos y+\sin y+(\cos x+\sin x-\cos y+\sin y)i=0,\]
so  $\cos x-\sin x+\cos y+\sin y=0$  and  $\cos x+\sin x-\cos y+\sin y=0$ . Since  $P=0,Q=0\Leftrightarrow P-Q=0,P+Q=0$ , this is equivalent to  $\cos x-\sin y=0$  and  $\cos y-\sin x=0$ . Notice that
\[\cos x-\sin y=0\implies \cos x=\cos (270-y)\implies x+y=270\text{ or } y-x=270\text{ or }y-x=-90,\]
assuming we restrict  $0\le x,y<360$ . Similarly we get  $x+y=270$  or  $y-x=90$  or  $y-x=-270$  for  $\cos y-\sin x=0$ . The only case where both of these holds is when  $x+y=270$ , which corresponds to  $\angle A+\angle B=135$ . Thus we get another 134 possibilities. 

The answer is  $89+134=\boxed{223}$ .</details>

stem_md: For any set  $S$ , let  $P(S)$  be its power set, the set of all of its subsets. Over all sets  $A$  of  $2015$  arbitrary finite sets, let  $N$  be the maximum possible number of ordered pairs  $(S,T)$  such that  $S \in P(A), T \in P(P(A))$ ,  $S \in T$ , and  $S \subseteq T$ . (Note that by convention, a set may never contain itself.) Find the remainder when  $N$  is divided by  $1000.$ *Proposed by Ashwin Sah*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>For a pair of sets  $(S, T)$  such that  $S$  is a subset of  $A$  and  $T$  is a collection of subsets of  $A$ , if it is true that  $S \subseteq T$ , then  $S$  itself is also a collection of subsets of  $A$ . Thus every element of  $S$  would be a subset of  $A$ .

Therefore, to maximize the number of such pairs  $(S, T)$ , we need to maximize the number of elements of  $A$  that are also subsets of  $A$ . It would be especially nice if, for all  $a \in A$ ,  $a \subseteq A$ . That would mean that we won't have to worry about elements of  $S$  not being subsets of  $A$ , so any  $S$  could be part of a pair  $(S, T)$  so long as we select a suitable superset  $T$  that contains both  $S$  and the elements of  $S$ .

There is, in fact, such a set  $A$  for which  $a \in A$  implies  $a \subseteq A$ . If you have ever heard of the [set-theoretic definition of natural numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set-theoretic_definition_of_natural_numbers),  $A$  could essentially be the set that is the natural number 2015. If we define  $0$  to be equal to the empty set  $\{\}$  and recursively define  $n+1$  to be equal to  $n \cup \{n\}$  (so  $1 = \{\{\}\} = \{0\}, 2 = \{\{\}, \{\{\}\}\} = \{0, 1\}$  and so on) one can see that for all such natural numbers  $n = \{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$ . But note that with this definition, the  $\in$  relation is equivalent to the  $<$  relation and the  $\subseteq$  relation, provided that the two sets being related are both natural numbers defined in this way, is equivalent to the  $\le$  relation. Thus  $k \in n$  implies  $k < n$  which in turn implies  $k \leq n$  which in turn implies  $k \subseteq n$ . Thus if  $A = 2015$ , for all  $S \in A$ ,  $S \subseteq A$ .

Now let  $|S| = n$ . Then for each  $S$ , we attempt to construct  $T$ , subset of the power set of  $A$ , such that  $S \in T$  and  $S \subseteq T$ . That means there are at least  $n+1$  subsets of  $A$  that  $T$  must contain. This leaves another  $2^{2015}-n-1$  subsets of  $A$  that  $T$  may or may not contain, giving a total of  $2^{2^{2015}-n-1}$  supersets of  $S$  and subsets of the power set of  $A$  that could be potential  $T$ 's.

As there are  $\binom{2015}{n}$  subsets of size  $n$  of  $A$ ,  we seek  $\sum_{n=0}^{2015} \binom{2015}{n}2^{2^{2015} - n - 1}$ . We can simplify this as \[ 2^{2^{2015}-1}\sum_{n=0}^{2015}\binom{2015}{n}2^{-n} = 2^{2^{2015}-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right)^{2015} = 2^{2^{2015}-2016}\cdot 3^{2015} \] with the binomial theorem. From there we can find that this is equivalent to 872 mod 1000.</details>

stem_md:
Toner Drum and Celery Hilton are both running for president. A total of  $2015$  people cast their vote, giving  $60\%$  to Toner Drum. Let  $N$  be the number of "representative'' sets of the  $2015$  voters that could have been polled to correctly predict the winner of the election (i.e. more people in the set voted for Drum than Hilton). Compute the remainder when  $N$  is divided by  $2017$ .

*Proposed by Ashwin Sah*
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>We use the generating function  $(1+x)^{1209}(1+1/x)^{806}=\dfrac{(1+x)^{2015}}{x^{806}}$ . We want the sum of the coefficients of all the terms with positive exponent on x, which is  $\sum_{k=807}^{2015}\binom{2015}{k}$ . Notice that
\[\binom{2015}{k}=\dfrac{2015\times2014\times\dotsm(2016-k)}{1\times2\times3\dotsm k}\equiv\dfrac{(-2)(-3)\dotsm(-1-k)}{1\times2\times\dotsm k}\equiv(-1)^k(k+1)\pmod{2017}.\]
Thus the answer is  $\sum_{k=807}^{2015}(-1)^k(k+1)=-1412\equiv\boxed{605}\pmod{2017}$ .</details>

stem_md:
Given an integer  $n$ , an integer  $1 \le a \le n$  is called  $n$ -*well* if \[ \left\lfloor\frac{n}{\left\lfloor n/a \right\rfloor}\right\rfloor = a. \] Let  $f(n)$  be the number of  $n$ -well numbers, for each integer  $n \ge 1$ . Compute  $f(1) + f(2) + \ldots + f(9999)$ .

*Proposed by Ashwin Sah*
solution_md:
Nobody actually posted a justified solution, so here's the idea:
<details><summary>Mostly a Solution</summary>For  $n$ , the numbers which are  $n$ -well are  $\left\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\right\rfloor$  for  $1 \le i \le n$ ; notice that there are repeats!

First of all, an  $n$ -well number  $a$  is obviously of the form  $a = \left\lfloor\frac{n}{b}\right\rfloor$ , because just let  $b = \left\lfloor\frac{n}{a}\right\rfloor$ .

Also,  $\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\right\rfloor}\right\rfloor}\right\rfloor = \left\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\right\rfloor$  when  $1 \le i \le n$ , so all these guys work.

To count the amount actually in this list, notice that  $1, 2, \ldots, \left\lfloor\sqrt{n}\right\rfloor$  are obviously in the list. Then, so are  $\left\lfloor\frac{n}{b}\right\rfloor$  for  $1 \le b \le \left\lfloor\sqrt{n}\right\rfloor$ , and these are actually all of them. So it's like approximately  $2\sqrt{n}$ ; the specifics can be found out by case-checking or by looking for a pattern.

Also, this characterization/solution trivializes **ABCDE**'s generalization:  $n$ -well-well-...-well numbers are the same as  $n$ -well numbers.

And if  $n = p - 1$  for  $p \ge 5$  a prime... you get stuff related to a certain RMM problem.</details>

stem_md:
Amandine and Brennon play a turn-based game, with Amadine starting.
On their turn, a player must select a positive integer which cannot be represented as a sum of multiples of any of the previously selected numbers.
For example, if  $3, 5$  have been selected so far, only  $1, 2, 4, 7$  are available to be picked;
if only  $3$  has been selected so far, all numbers not divisible by three are eligible.
A player loses immediately if they select the integer  $1$ .

Call a number  $n$  *feminist* if  $\gcd(n, 6) = 1$  and if Amandine wins if she starts with  $n$ . Compute the sum of the *feminist* numbers less than  $40$ .

*Proposed by Ashwin Sah*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Suppose that two coprime numbers  $m$  and  $n$  were already picked, not equal to 2 or 3 (You can verify that if someone picks 2 or 3 they immediately lose because the other player picks the other one, then the first player is forced to pick 1). Then the set of remaining choices is finite, and let the maximum be  $M$ . If a number  $s\neq M$  is picked, then you can show that there exists a nonnegative linear combination of  $m$ , $n$ , and  $s$  that equals  $M$ .

Suppose the player about to move in this finite set was going to lose; then if he picks  $M$ , the second player has a winning  $s\neq M$ , but the first player could have just picked this  $s$  in the first place, putting himself in the winning position since picking  $s$  also deletes  $M$ . Therefore whoever is forced to pick a number coprime to something already picked will lose because the next player will have a winning strategy. This can be forced by picking a prime that's not 2 or 3.

Thus Amandine wins on all the primes, and loses on the numbers 25 and 35 because Brennon responds with 5 and then Amandine will lose, giving a sum of  $\boxed{192}$</details>

stem_md:
Let  $p = 2017,$  a prime number. Let  $N$  be the number of ordered triples  $(a,b,c)$  of integers such that  $1 \le a,b \le p(p-1)$  and  $a^b-b^a=p \cdot c$ . Find the remainder when  $N$  is divided by  $1000000.$ *Proposed by Evan Chen and Ashwin Sah*

*Remark:* The problem was initially proposed for  $p = 3,$  and  $1 \le a, b \le 30.$
solution_md:
We have  $a^b\equiv b^a\mod p$ . If  $p|a$  then  $p|b$ , and all such  $a$ ,  $b$  work. There are  $p-1$  multiples of  $p$  from  $1$  to  $p(p-1)$ , so there are  $(p-1)^2$  solutions for  $a$  and  $b$  when  $p|a$ .

Assume  $p\nmid a$ . We're going to count the number of  $b$ 's that work for a fixed  $a$  and sum over all  $a$  with  $1\le a\le p(p-1)$  and  $p\nmid a$ . We have  $a^b\equiv b^a\mod p$ . If we fix  $b\mod p-1$ , then  $a^b\mod p$  is fixed by FLT. If we fix  $b\mod p$ , then  $b^a\mod p$  is fixed. Furthermore, if we pair a residue class  $\mod p-1$  with a residue class  $\mod p$ , we get exactly one residue class  $\mod p(p-1)$  by CRT. So we're going to see which residue classes  $\mod p-1$  work for  $b$ , see how many residue classes  $\mod p$  work for  $b$  for each residue class  $\mod p-1$ , and sum. Let  $g$  be a primitive root  $\mod p$ . Then  $a\equiv g^x\mod p$  and  $b\equiv g^y\mod p$  for some integers  $x$  and  $y$ . Essentially we need  $y$  to satisfy  $g^{xb}\equiv g^{ay}\mod p$ , or  $xb\equiv ay\mod p-1$ . (Remember, we are choosing  $b\mod p-1$  so that there exists a solution to this congruence for  $y$ .) So what kind of residue classes  $\mod p-1$  for  $b$  work? We have  $p-1|ay-bx$ . Let  $k=\gcd(a, p-1)$ . Note that  $k|p-1|ay-bx$  and  $k|ay$ , so  $k|bx$ . This is equivalent to  $\tfrac{k}{\gcd(k, x)}|b$ . So any residue class  $\mod p-1$  that is "divisible" by  $\tfrac{k}{\gcd(k, x)}$  works. Conversely, if  $k|bx$ , then the divisibility  $p-1|ay-bx$  is equivalent to  $\tfrac{p-1}{k}|\tfrac{a}{k}y-\tfrac{bx}{k}$ , which has exactly one solution  $\mod \tfrac{p-1}{k}$  because  $\gcd(\tfrac{a}{k},\tfrac{p-1}{k})=1$ , which is  $k$  solutions  $\mod p-1$ . And these are solutions for  $y$ , the exponent of  $g$  for  $b$ , so each of these solutions translates to exactly one solution for  $b\mod p$ , and there are no other solutions for  $b\mod p$ . So we get exactly  $k$  solutions  $\mod p-1$  for  $y$ , i.e.  $k$  solutions  $\mod p$  for  $b$ , whenever  $\tfrac{k}{\gcd(k, x)}|b$ , and  $0$  solutions otherwise. How many residue classes  $\mod p-1$  are divisible by  $\tfrac{k}{\gcd(k, x)}$ ? Just  $\tfrac{(p-1)\gcd(k, x)}{k}$ . We just got that each of these residue classes yields  $k$  solutions  $\mod p$  and every other residue class yields  $0$  solutions, so multiplying by  $k$  gives  $(p-1)\gcd(k, x)$ .

Note that since  $a\equiv g^x\mod p$ , we have that  $a^{\text{ord}_p(a)}\equiv g^{x\text{ord}_p(a)}\equiv 1\mod p$ . So  $p-1|x\text{ord}_p(a)$ . Since  $\text{ord}_p(a)|p-1$ , we have that  $\tfrac{p-1}{\text{ord}_p(a)}|x$ . Also,  $\text{ord}_p(a)$  is the least positive integer  $t$  such that  $a^t\equiv 1\mod p$ , so if \[\dfrac{x}{(\tfrac{p-1}{\text{ord}_p(a)})}\] shares a factor  $d>1$  with  $p-1$ , then  $a^{\text{ord}_p(a)/d}\equiv 1\mod p$ , which contradicts the minimality of  $\text{ord}_p(a)$ . So it must be coprime to  $p-1$ . Since  $k|p-1$ , we have that  $\gcd(k, x)=\gcd(k, \tfrac{p-1}{\text{ord}_p(a)})$  since  $x$  only adds factors coprime to  $p-1$ , which won't change the  $\gcd$ . Since  $k=\gcd(a, p-1)$ , this equals  $\gcd(\gcd(a, p-1),\tfrac{p-1}{\text{ord}_p(a)})$ . So what are we really doing? We are taking the  $\gcd$  of  $a$  and  $p-1$ , and then we are taking the  $\gcd$  of that result with a factor of  $p-1$ . That's the same as taking the  $\gcd$  of  $a$  and the factor of  $p-1$ , since anything extra that the  $p-1$  might contribute is just taken away by the factor of  $p-1$ . So this is really just  $\gcd(a, \tfrac{p-1}{\text{ord}_p(a)})$ , so there are exactly  $(p-1)\gcd(a,\tfrac{p-1}{\text{ord}_p(a)})$  total solutions for  $b$ . (For a fixed  $a$ , that is.)

So now we just have to sum over all  $a$  with  $1\le a\le p(p-1)$  and  $p\nmid a$ , add in  $(p-1)^2$  for  $p|a$ , and we're done. But the sum is tricky: \[\displaystyle\sum_{1\le a\le p(p-1), p\nmid a}(p-1)\gcd(a,\tfrac{p-1}{\text{ord}_p(a)})\] We are going to use the CRT idea again: we will first range through the residue classes  $\mod p$  for  $a$ , then through the residue classes  $\mod p-1$ . First we will use the fact that for every divisor  $d$  of  $p-1$ , there are exactly  $\phi(d)$  guys with order  $d$ . (And of course if  $d$  is not a divisor of  $p-1$ , there are  $0$  guys with order  $d$ .) You prove this using the fact/proving that there exists a primitive root. So basically, we are going to sum over  $d=\text{ord}_p(a)$  instead. Since there are  $\phi(d)$  different values for  $a$  with order  $d$ , the sum becomes \[(p-1)\displaystyle\sum_{d|p-1}\left(\phi(d)\displaystyle\sum_{1\le a\le p-1}\gcd(a,\tfrac{p-1}{d})\right)\] where the inner sum comes from the fact that  $a$  still needs to range through the residue classes  $\mod p-1$ . To compute the inner sum, note that once  $a$  reaches above  $\tfrac{p-1}{d}$ ,  $\gcd(a, \tfrac{p-1}{d})$  equals  $\gcd(a-\tfrac{p-1}{d}, \tfrac{p-1}{d})$ , so the inner sum is really just \[\displaystyle\sum_{1\le a\le \tfrac{p-1}{d}}\gcd(a, \tfrac{p-1}{d})\] added  $d$  times in succession. So our total sum becomes \[(p-1)\displaystyle\sum_{d|p-1}\left(\phi(d)d\displaystyle\sum_{1\le a\le\tfrac{p-1}{d}}\gcd(a, \tfrac{p-1}{d})\right)\] To compute the inner sum, sum instead over  $\gcd(a, \tfrac{p-1}{d})=e$ : there are exactly  $\phi(\tfrac{p-1}{ed})$  guys  $x$  less than or equal to  $\tfrac{p-1}{d}$  with  $\gcd(x, \tfrac{p-1}{d})=e$ . So now our sum is \[(p-1)\displaystyle\sum_{d|p-1}\left(\phi(d)d\displaystyle\sum_{e|\tfrac{p-1}{d}}e\phi(\tfrac{p-1}{ed})\right)=(p-1)\displaystyle\sum_{d|p-1}\sum_{e|\tfrac{p-1}{d}}\left(\phi(d)ed\phi(\tfrac{p-1}{ed})\right)\] Since  $e|\tfrac{p-1}{d}$ , we have that  $de|p-1$ . So instead we can let  $f=de$  run through the divisors of  $p-1$ , and let  $d$  run through the divisors of  $f$ : \[(p-1)\displaystyle\sum_{f|p-1}f\phi\left(\dfrac{p-1}{f}\right)\sum_{d|f}\phi(d)\] But  $\sum_{d|n}\phi(d)=n$  for any natural number  $n$ , so the sum is \[(p-1)\displaystyle\sum_{f|p-1}f^2\phi\left(\dfrac{p-1}{f}\right)\] I couldn't simplify this any further, so I computed it directly.

stem_md:
Define  $\left\lVert A-B \right\rVert = (x_A-x_B)^2+(y_A-y_B)^2$  for every two points  $A = (x_A, y_A)$  and  $B = (x_B, y_B)$  in the plane.
Let  $S$  be the set of points  $(x,y)$  in the plane for which  $x,y \in \left\{ 0,1,\dots,100 \right\}$ .
Find the number of functions  $f : S \to S$  such that  $\left\lVert A-B \right\rVert \equiv \left\lVert f(A)-f(B) \right\rVert \pmod{101}$  for any  $A, B \in S$ .

*Proposed by Victor Wang*
solution_md:
SolutionThis is equivalent to finding all functions $f:\mathbb{F}_{101}[\text{i}]\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{101}[\text{i}]$ such that $|a-b|^2=|f(a)-f(b)|^2\pmod{101}$ . Scale everything so $f(0)=0$ , which gives us a factor of $\boxed{101^2}$ so far. Now note that we have $|a|^2=|f(a)|^2\pmod{101}$ . Thus, $|+10xi|^2=|f(1+10i)|^2=0\pmod{101}$ . Thus, for some real $r$ , it follows $f(1+10i)=r+10ri$ or $f(1+10i)=r-10ri$ . Suppose $f(x)=g(x)+i\cdot h(x)$ . Then note that $f(x)=g(x)-i\cdot h(x)$ is also a solution. Thus, assume that $f(1+10i)=r+10ri$ , which gives us an extra factor of $\boxed{2}$ . It's easy to check $r\neq 0$ ; just check that $|1+10i-1|^2=|0-f(1)|^2\pmod{101}$ is false, using $1=|f(1)|^2\pmod{101}$ . Suppose for some real $x\neq 0$ , we had $f(x+10xi)=y-10yi$ for some real $y$ . Then $0=|x+10xi-1-10i|^2=|f(x+10xi)-f(1+10i)|^2=|y-r+i(-10y-10r)i|^2\pmod{101}$ which means that $(y-r)^2+(10y+10r)^2=0\pmod{101}$ or $yr=0\pmod{101}$ . Note that $r\neq 0$ , and you can see that $|x+10xi-x|^2=|0-f(x)|^2\pmod{101}$ gives a contradiction, so $y\neq 0$ , so $yr=0\pmod{101}$ is a contradiction. Great, now we know that $f(x+10xi)=y+10yi$ for all real $x$ . We actually claim that $\frac{f(x+10xi)}{x+10xi}$ is a constant. Suppose $f(x+10xi)=y+10yi$ and $f(1)=a+bi$ . Note that $|f(x+10xi)-f(1)|=|(x-1)+10xi|^2\pmod{101}$ gives us $(y-a)^2+(10y-b)^2=(x-1)^2+100x^2$ . Since $a^2+b^2=1\pmod{101}$ this implies that $-2ay-20yb=-2x\pmod{101}$ or $y(a+10b)=x\pmod{101}$ . Thus, $\frac{x}{y}=\frac{x+10xi}{f(x+10xi)}$ is constant. More importantly, note this means $\frac{f(x+10xi)}{x+10xi}=r$ since $\frac{f(1+10i)}{1+10i}=r$ by definition. We now claim that $f(1-10i)=\frac{1}{r}-\frac{10}{r}i$ . Using similar reasoning that we used to show $f(x+10xi)$ is of form $y+10yi$ , note that it follows $f(1-10i)=z-10zi$ for some real constant $z$ . Then $|(1+10i)-(1-10i)|^2=|f(1+10i)-f(1-10i)|^2\pmod{101}$ or $-4=(r-z)^2+(10r+10z)^2\pmod{101}$ . This gives us $rz=1\pmod{101}$ so $z=\frac{1}{r}$ and $f(1-10i)=\frac{1}{r}-\frac{10}{r}i$ . Now, for the home stretch. Suppose $f(x+yi)=u+vi$ . then $(r-u)^2+(10r-v)^2=(1-x)^2+(10-y)^2$ . but $x^2+y^2=u^2+v^2$ so $-2ru-20rv=-2x-20y$ or $r(u+10v)=x+10y$ . On the other hand, $(1/r-u)^2+(-10/r-v)^2=(1-x)^2+(-10-y)^2$ . thus $-2u/r+20v/r=-2x+20y$ or $1/r(u-10v)=x-10y$ . Thus it follows $u=\frac{1/r(x+10y)+r(x-10y)}{2}$ and $v=\frac{1/r(x+10y)-r(x-10y)}{20}$ . So $f(x+yi)=\frac{1/r(x+10y)+r(x-10y)}{2}+i\cdot \frac{1/r(x+10y)-r(x-10y)}{20}$ . We can check that this works for all nonzero $r$ , which gives a factor of $\boxed{100}$ for our count. Thus, the answer is clearly $100^2\cdot 2\cdot 100$ or $2000000$ . And there goes all that work :( The end.

Hint$f$ is bijective: Here is a quick sketch: Say that $(x_1,y_1)\rightarrow (a,b)$ and $(x_2,y_2)\rightarrow (a,b)$ then for all other points $(x,y)$ , $(x-x_1)^2+(y-y_1)^2=(x-x_2)^2+(y-y_2)^2$ mod $101$ , which clearly is impossible (a rigorous argument is possible by using $(x,y)=(x_1,y_2)$ or something).
SolutionFirst, let the points be vectors and let origin be $(0, 0)$ . Without loss of generality let $f(O) = O$ , as long as we multiply by $101^2$ in the end. Technique: We will first reduce the condition using vectors and $f(O) = O$ to something easier to deal with. Then we can prove that the vectors $f(x, 0)$ are collinear and thus $f(x, 0) = x f(1, 0)$ ; similarly $f(0, y) = y f(0, 1)$ . Now, the fact $f(1, 0) \cdot f(0, 1) \equiv 0$ and that they are unit vectors shows that $f(0, 1), f(1, 0)$ are linearly independent, so we can prove that $f(x, y) = x f(1, 0) + y f(0, 1)$ , so $f$ is defined solely by $f(1, 0), f(0, 1)$ . Lemma. If $a \cdot b \equiv c \cdot b \equiv 0 \pmod {101}$ with $b \neq 0$ , then $a = kc$ for some $k$ . Proof. Based on the fact that $F_{101}$ is a field, so two vectors are linearly dependent if and only if they are collinear. Now notice that the condition is $(a - b)^2 \equiv (f(a) - f(b))^2$ . By using $b = O$ , we have $a^2 = f(a)^2$ . Hence we have $$ a \cdot b \equiv f(A) \cdot f(B) \pmod {101}. $$ The cool thing is that if we let $a = (x, 0)$ and $b = (0, 1)$ , then $f(x, 0) \cdot f(0, 1) \equiv 0$ , so by Lemma and the fact that $f(0, 1) \neq 0$ by bijectivity, we have $f(x, 0) \equiv g(x) f(1, 0)$ for some function $g$ . Similarly, $f(0, y) = h(y) f(0, 1)$ for some function $h$ . But notice that $(x, 0) \cdot (1, 0) = f(x, 0) \cdot f(1, 0)$ , so $g(x) f(1, 0) \cdot f(1, 0) = x$ . Because $f(1, 0)^2 = (1, 0)^2 = 1$ , we have $g(x) = x$ for all $x$ . Similarly $h(y) = y$ for all $y$ . We also know that $f(1, 0) \cdot f(0, 1) = 0$ and $f(1, 0)^2 = f(0, 1)^2 = 1$ , so they form a unit basis in $F_{101}$ . (If $a f(1, 0) + b f(0, 1) \equiv O$ , then squaring yields $a^2 + b^2 \equiv 0 \pmod {101}$ ; also, $a f(1, 0) \equiv -b f(0, 1)$ and squaring yields $a^2 \equiv b^2 \pmod {101}$ , so $a \equiv b \equiv 0 \pmod {101}$ , meaning that $f(1, 0), f(0, 1)$ are linearly independent.) Notice that $(f(x, y) - f(x, 0)) \cdot f(1, 0) \equiv 0$ , so since $f(0, y) \cdot f(1, 0) = 0$ , we have $f(x, y) = f(x, 0) + k f(0, y)$ for some $k$ . Similarly $f(x, y) = f(0, y) + m f(x, 0)$ for some $m$ . Because $f(1, 0)$ and $f(0, 1)$ are linearly independent, so are $f(x, 0)$ and $f(0, y)$ , and so $k = m = 1$ . Thus $f(x, y) = f(x, 0) + f(0, y) = x f(1, 0) + y f(0, 1)$ and so it suffices to count the number of orthogonal unit bases of $F_{101}$ . But this is easy. Indeed, the equation $a^2 + b^2 \equiv 1 \pmod {101}$ is equivalent to $(a + 10b)(a - 10b) \equiv 1 \pmod {101}$ , so $a + 10b = x$ ad $a - 10b = x^{-1}$ for some nonzero $x$ . Because each choice of $x$ yields a unique $(a, b)$ , there are $100$ valid solutions $(a, b) = F(1, 0)$ . Now there are 2 choices for $F(0, 1)$ , so there are $2 \cdot 100 \cdot 101^2 = 2040200$ functions total. (Oh yeah we have to verify whether all such functions work, and the answer is they satisfy the condition $a \cdot b = f(a) \cdot f(b)$ , so they work. :) )

Now  $Q((1, 0), (0, 0))$  and  $Q((0, 1), (0, 0))$  give  $a^2+c^2\equiv b^2+d^2\equiv 1$ , so  $b^2 \equiv c^2$  and  $a^2 \equiv d^2$ . Since  $101\equiv1 \pmod{4}$ , this means  $c \equiv \pm b$  and  $a \equiv \pm d$ . Now  $P(1, 1)$  gives  $ab \equiv -cd$ , so  $c \equiv \pm a, d \equiv \mp b$  (we have to be a bit careful about the case where  $a$  or  $b$  is 0, but it all works out. We can check that this is in fact a solution. The number of ways to pick  $a,b$  such that  $a^2+b^2 \equiv 1$  is 100, and we must multiply by 2 because the signs of  $c$  and  $d$  have two possibilities, so our final answer is  $100 \cdot 2 \cdot 101^2 = 2040200$ .</details>

stem_md:
Let  $W = \ldots x_{-1}x_0x_1x_2 \ldots$  be an infinite periodic word consisting of only the letters  $a$  and  $b$ . The minimal period of  $W$  is  $2^{2016}$ . Say that a word  $U$  *appears* in  $W$  if there are indices  $k \le \ell$  such that  $U = x_kx_{k+1} \ldots x_{\ell}$ . A word  $U$  is called *special* if  $Ua, Ub, aU, bU$  all appear in  $W$ . (The empty word is considered special) You are given that there are no special words of length greater than 2015.

	Let  $N$  be the minimum possible number of special words. Find the remainder when  $N$  is divided by  $1000$ .
*Proposed by Yang Liu*
solution_md:
<details><summary>#22 PROOF by suli</summary>Suppose there exists a  $2016$ -letter word that does not appear in  $W$ . By the Pigeonhole Principle there exist two distinct indices  $k, m$  such that the  $2016$ -letter words starting with  $x_k$  and with  $x_m$  must be the same. Now because no  $2016$ -letter word is special, either the corresponding letter after each word or the corresponding letter before each word must be the same. Then we have congruent  $2017$ -letter words, and repeat process to form congruent  $2018$ -letter words, etc., contradicting periodicity. Thus all  $2016$ -letter words appear in  $W$  and this holds for  $n$ -letter words with  $n \le 2016$  as well, so all such  $n$ -letter words are special.</details>
<details><summary>#22 PROOF by vincenthuang</summary>we claim every block of length  $l$  with  $l \le 2016$  must appear sometime in  $W$ . If we prove it for  $l=2016$ , we have proven the entire claim.

Assume this is not true, so in the  $2^{2016}$  possible sequences of length  $2016$ , there are only  $2^{2016}-1$  choices, so some word appears  $2$  times. 

Now let this string be  $a_1a_2...a_{2016}$  and  $a_{n+1}a_{n+2}..a_{n+2016}$ . Note that it cannot be a special word, so basically the two occurrences of this string must have the same preceding letter or same succeeding letter. WLOG assume they both have succeeding letter  $1$ .

Now take  $a_1a_2..a_{2016}1$  and it appears twice, do the same thing. Basically we grow sequences from these two identical ones and get period less than  $2^{2016}$ , contradiction.

So every string of length  $\le 2016$  always appears. So take any string of length  $2015$  or less and it's clear that it works.

So we get  $2^0+2^1+...+2^{2015} = 2^{2016}-1$  which yields  $535$ .</details>

stem_md:
For integers  $0 \le m,n \le 64$ , let  $\alpha(m,n)$  be the number of nonnegative integers  $k$  for which  $\left\lfloor m/2^k \right\rfloor$  and  $\left\lfloor n/2^k \right\rfloor$  are both odd integers.  Consider a  $65 \times 65$  matrix  $M$  whose  $(i,j)$ th entry (for  $1 \le i, j \le 65$ ) is \[ (-1)^{\alpha(i-1, j-1)}. \] Compute the remainder when  $\det M$  is divided by  $1000$ .

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $A_n$  be the  $2^n \times 2^n$  matrix with entries  $a_{ij} = (-1)^{\alpha(i-1, j-1)}.$ Notice that  $\alpha(i, j)$  is the XOR function of  $i$  and  $j$  in binary, and we care about it  $\pmod 2$ . Thus,  $a_{ij} = a_{i(j+2^{n-1})} = a_{(i+2^{n-1})j} = -a_{(i+2^{n-1})(j+2^{n-1})}.$ Now, divide the matrix  $A_n$  into quadrants. By adding row  $i + 2^{n-1}$  to row  $i$  for each  $1 \le i \le 2^{n-1}$ , we make quadrant II (the upper left) equal to twice its original value, and quadrant I (the upper right) is all zeros. By taking out the  $2$  from the first  $2^{n-1}$  rows, we obtain a matrix that is the same as  $A_n$  except with quadrant I all zero. Now add row  $i$  to row  $i + 2^{n-1}$  for each  $1 \le i \le 2^{n-1}$  to make quadrant III all zeros, and factor out the  $(-1)$  from each of the last  $2^{n-1}$  rows to obtain a matrix of the form  $A_{n-1} | 0; 0 | A_{n-1}$ . This has determinant  $|A_{n-1}|^2$ , and so  $$ |A_n| = (-2)^{2^{n-1}} |A_{n-1}|^2. $$  If  $|A_n| = 2^{b_n}$  (since  $|A_1| = -2$ , by convention define  $b_1 = 1$ ), then we have  $$ b_n = 2^{n-1} + 2b_{n-1}, $$  so  $b_1 = 1, b_2 = 4, b_3 = 12, b_4 = 32, b_5 = 80, \dots, b_n = n 2^{n-1}$ . Hence, we want  $$ -2|A_6| = -2 \cdot 2^{6 \cdot 2^5} = -2^{193} \pmod {1000}. $$   $\pmod 8$  gives  $0$ , and  $\pmod {125}$  gives  $-2^{-7} \equiv -128^{-1} \equiv -3^{-1} \equiv -42 \equiv 208 \pmod {125}$ , so the answer is  $208$ .</details>

Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle with incenter  $I$ ; ray  $AI$  meets the circumcircle  $\Omega$  of  $ABC$  at  $M \neq A$ . Suppose  $T$  lies on line  $BC$  such that  $\angle MIT=90^{\circ}$ .
Let  $K$  be the foot of the altitude from  $I$  to  $\overline{TM}$ . Given that  $\sin B = \frac{55}{73}$  and  $\sin C = \frac{77}{85}$ , and  $\frac{BK}{CK} = \frac mn$  in lowest terms, compute  $m+n$ .

*Proposed by Evan Chen*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $K'$  be the point on the circumcircle of  $ABC$  with  $IK'\perp MK'$ . By radical axis on the circumcircle of  $ABC$ , the circumcircle of  $BIC$ , and the circumcircle of  $IK'M$ , we have that  $T$  lies on  $IK'$ , or  $K\equiv K'$ .

Now, note that  $KI$  intersects the circumcircle of  $ABC$  again at the opposite point of  $M$ , so  $K$  is the mixtillinear tangency point.

To compute  $BK/CK$ , note that it suffices to compute the cross ratio  $(A,K;B,C)$ . Reflecting over the angle bisector of  $A$  and projecting onto  $BC$ , it suffices to compute  $(D,P_{\infty};B,C)$ , where  $D$  is the tangency point of the  $A$ -excircle with  $BC$ . But since we know the sines of the angles, we can compute the lengths of the triangle and finish.</details>
